name: DicePool Lab
idea: No-code visual calculator that gives exact odds for custom tabletop dice mechanics (success pools, push/reroll, exploding, keep/drop, roll-under opposed rolls, mixed results).
description: A GM or game designer builds a roll from blocks (pool size, success threshold, push once, explode on max, drop N failures, roll-under vs opposed) and instantly sees exact probability tables such as 'at least 2 successes with N dice, pushed or not', plus a side-by-side comparison of two characters. Results are shareable by link and printable for a GM screen. Hard to copy because the engine has to get stateful mechanics exactly right (push re-rolls, die-vs-die elimination, bounded explosions, crit-on-match) and ship presets for real systems, while the incumbent AnyDice needs its own scripting language.
capital_note: Domain only; everything else on free tiers.
why_hard_to_copy: Correctness-critical probability engine for mechanics that generic dice roller libraries do not model, plus a curated library of system presets (Year Zero, Blades-style, d100 roll-under, etc.).
web_delivery: Pure client-side SPA on Vercel hobby (TypeScript exact-distribution engine, config encoded in the URL); Supabase free only for optional saved presets.
satellite_what: One static page per popular dice system (Year Zero / Vaesen push odds, Blades-style pools, d100 roll-under) with the engine preloaded.
marketing_where: RPG Stack Exchange (answer on-topic probability questions and link the tool); ENWorld and GiantITP forums dice-math threads; itch.io TTRPG game-jam and devlog communities; Discord servers of indie TTRPG designers
marketing_target: Homebrew GMs and indie tabletop designers tuning difficulty
marketing_funnel: Search or forum answer -> preset odds page -> custom builder -> shareable link that other designers open
cold_outreach: Message creators of small Year Zero / Blades hacks on itch.io offering a ready-made odds table for their core roll.
post_ideas: Exact odds of the Vaesen push mechanic for 1-10 dice (table) | Why 'roll under, both succeed' opposed d100 rolls favour the higher skill more than you think | Built a visual AnyDice alternative for dice pools - feedback wanted
competitors: AnyDice; Icepool; Contract RPG dice pool calculator
notes: Strongest demand cluster in my sweep: six independent RPG.SE questions in about nine months plus a softwarerecs request. Doubt: a free tool for hobbyists has weak direct monetization (ads, donations, or a pro tier for saved/shared systems). AnyDice is the entrenched incumbent, so the wedge is no-code plus push/opposed/mixed-result blocks.

name: Takeout Doctor
idea: Browser tool that checks, repairs and organizes huge Google Photos / iCloud export zips locally before you move to Immich or a NAS.
description: You pick the downloaded Takeout zip parts and an output folder. It verifies every part is present and not corrupt, pairs photos with their JSON sidecars (including truncated and renamed files), restores capture dates and GPS, rebuilds albums and removes the duplicate copies Takeout makes. Nothing is uploaded. Hard to copy because of multi-GB zip streaming in the browser and the long tail of Takeout naming and metadata edge cases.
why_hard_to_copy: Correctness-critical handling of multi-GB zips, sidecar matching rules (truncated names, -edited suffixes, duplicate album copies, Live Photos) and in-browser EXIF/XMP writing; a weekend prompt-built version breaks on real exports.
web_delivery: Static web app on Vercel using File System Access API (Chromium) to read zip parts with Blob.slice and write the organized output to a chosen folder; no server, no uploads; Supabase only for optional anonymous bug reports.
satellite_what: Free page: drop all downloaded Takeout zip parts and it checks the numbering is complete and every zip entry passes its CRC, then lists which parts to re-download.
marketing_where: Immich GitHub Discussions and Discord; Lemmy c/selfhosted and c/privacy; Hacker News Show HN; Google Photos Help Community threads; AlternativeTo listing
marketing_target: People leaving Google Photos or iCloud for Immich, Synology, a NAS or local folders.
marketing_funnel: Free part checker -> full organizer (free for small exports, one-time unlock for large ones).
cold_outreach: Reply with the checker link in threads where someone reports corrupted or missing Takeout parts.
post_ideas: Your Google Takeout may be missing files: check it in your browser, nothing uploaded | Why Takeout photos lose dates and GPS and how to restore them | Moving from iCloud Photos with albums intact: what the export really contains
competitors: GooglePhotosTakeoutHelper Neo; google-photo-meta-fixer; EXIF Metadata photo merger and organiser (Chrome extension); Metadata Fixer (vendor guide on Takeout via Drive + rclone); Ashampoo Meta Fusion
notes: Chromium-only for folder write-out; Safari/Firefox would need zip download fallback that hits memory limits. A Chrome extension and several CLIs already exist, so the web-app angle (zero install, verification first) is the differentiator. Takeout format can change without notice.

name: BackupPowerPlanner
idea: Plan home backup power: how long a power station runs your fridge, what generator you need, and how to wire it safely.
description: User picks appliances (with start-up surge and compressor duty cycle from a curated database), a power station or generator, and the cord or wire run; the tool outputs real runtime after inverter losses, whether surge fits, wire gauge and breaker for the distance, and notes about inlets and interlocks. The moat is the appliance surge and duty-cycle dataset plus electrical-code logic; generic vendor blogs and single-formula calculators miss surge and derating.
why_hard_to_copy: Curated appliance start-up and duty-cycle dataset, inverter and cord derating, plus NEC-style wire, breaker and interlock logic; error-prone for hobbyists to rebuild correctly.
web_delivery: Next.js PWA on Vercel; appliance and equipment data in Supabase; calculations in the browser, offline-capable for outages.
satellite_what: Enter battery Wh and fridge size to get realistic runtime with duty cycle and inverter loss.
marketing_where: Preparedness and off-grid forums; Solar and power-station owner Facebook groups; Hurricane-prep community pages; YouTube comment communities for power-station reviewers; Show HN
marketing_target: Homeowners in outage-prone areas, RV and off-grid users, DIY electricians
marketing_funnel: Search 'how long will a power station run my fridge' -> calculator -> planner.
cold_outreach: Email power-station review bloggers with an embeddable runtime widget.
post_ideas: How long does a 3,840 Wh power station really run a fridge? | Will your generator start your heat pump? Surge explained | Why your 200 ft extension cord is getting warm
competitors: Anker Solix fridge power station guide; Bluetti fridge runtime guide
notes: Six independent DIY-site questions with high views (2,226-3,219 for the top ones). Safety liability: must show code disclaimers and advise a licensed electrician for inlet and interlock work. Several single-formula calculators exist; the dataset and derating logic are the differentiator.

name: Gigbinder
idea: Offline-first web app for gigging bands: charts, setlists, transposition and band sync that does not break on every update.
description: Musicians keep PDF charts and ChordPro/lyric sheets in one place, build setlists, transpose with correct enharmonic spelling and capo hints, and run a full-screen stage mode that turns pages with a Bluetooth foot pedal (pedals send plain key presses, which browsers receive). Charts stay in the device (IndexedDB); only setlist order, keys and notes sync through Supabase so the whole band sees the same list. Hard to copy because of the chart-format importers (ChordPro, OnSong-style text, PDF), music-theory-correct transposition, and offline-first sync with conflict handling.
capital_note: Domain name only; Supabase free and Vercel hobby cover the rest.
why_hard_to_copy: Offline-first sync with conflict handling plus music-theory-correct transposition and several chart-format parsers; a CRUD setlist list is easy but a trustworthy stage tool is not.
web_delivery: PWA on Vercel; PDFs and text charts cached in IndexedDB via service worker; Supabase stores only small setlist and band-membership rows.
satellite_what: Free single-page tool: paste lyrics with chords, get any key, capo suggestions, printable one-page chart.
marketing_where: TalkBass and Gearspace forums; church worship-team and cover-band Facebook groups; Product Hunt and Show HN; Planning Center community
marketing_target: Gigging cover, wedding and worship bands who share charts across several devices
marketing_funnel: Free transposer page, then free binder for one band, then paid band-size tier later
cold_outreach: DM band leaders who posted about lost setlists or an app update that broke their charts, offering a free import from their old app.
post_ideas: I lost a year of setlists to an app update, so I built an offline-first binder | How a Bluetooth page-turner pedal works in a plain web page | Transposing without spelling disasters: why F# vs Gb matters on a chart
competitors: OnSong; forScore; Setlyst; Bandfix; Planning Center Music Stand; BandHelper; OnSong (OnSong Console web companion); SongbookPro / Charts by WorshipTools
notes: Strong repeated pattern across four apps in the last 3 months, but all signals are App Store reviews, so no engagement counts beyond review text. Real risk: musicians on iPads want native performance; Safari PWA storage eviction must be handled (ask for persistent storage, offer export). Competitor Setlyst already is a PWA.

name: DualPassport
idea: A rules guide for dual nationals and mixed-nationality families: which passport to show at check-in, security, border and EES lanes.
description: User picks their two nationalities, destination and route; the tool says which passport to present at airline check-in, at security, entering and leaving, how entry and exit records interact (for example US exit not being recorded), and what special rules apply (UK entitlement-certificate requirement, EU/EES lanes for mixed couples). The moat is the curated rules matrix by nationality pair and destination with cited sources; rules changed in 2025-2026 and general articles are dated.
why_hard_to_copy: Hand-curated rules matrix by nationality pair x destination with citations; fast-changing (EES, UK 2026 dual-national entry rule) so freshness is the barrier.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel; rules matrix in Supabase with source and verified_at; wizard flow client-side.
marketing_where: FlyerTalk forums; TripAdvisor destination forums; Travel Stack Exchange (answer questions, link only where site rules allow); Facebook expat and digital-nomad groups; Show HN; Product Hunt; Expat Facebook groups (Americans in Europe, British in Ireland, etc.)
marketing_target: Dual nationals, expat families, mixed-nationality couples
marketing_funnel: Search 'which passport to use dual citizen <route>' -> scenario page.
cold_outreach: Offer expat association newsletters a short checklist plus link.
post_ideas: UK dual nationals: the new entry rule explained | Which passport at airline check-in vs at the border? | Mixed EU/non-EU couple: which lane at EES?
competitors: The Local: rules for dual nationals travelling in Europe (2022); The Points Guy: how to use dual passports
notes: Six distinct askers, several with 1,000-4,200 views. Moat is freshness and citation quality. Informational travel-document guidance only, not legal advice; the coordinator may want to treat the 'legal services' ban as a risk here.

name: Batchbook
idea: Free web production planner for micro-bakeries and cottage food makers: scale formulas, check stock, plan the bake day, print allergen labels.
description: Recipes live as versioned formulas (baker's percentages, yield loss, ingredient densities) so one order list turns into a batch plan, a shopping list and a 'can I make X with what I have?' answer. It also builds the allergen matrix and a printable ingredient/allergen label for the maker's jurisdiction. Aimed at people launching a home or micro bakery who currently run it from spreadsheets; the moat is a curated ingredient-density, unit-conversion and label-rule dataset plus correct scaling math.
capital_note: Domain name only; Vercel hobby and Supabase free cover hosting.
why_hard_to_copy: Correct recipe scaling (baker's percentages, yield loss, volume-to-weight with ingredient densities) and jurisdiction-specific allergen/label rules are hand-curated data plus edge-case math, not CRUD. The open-source competitor is an Elixir app that non-developers cannot host.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel hobby, Supabase Postgres + RLS for recipes/orders; labels rendered to PDF client-side; installable PWA for use in the kitchen.
satellite_what: Single-page free calculator: paste a formula, scale to any dough weight or loaf count, convert cups/grams with ingredient densities.
marketing_where: The Fresh Loaf forum; Cottage food operator Facebook groups; Farmers market association newsletters; Product Hunt; Hacker News Show HN; Indie Hackers
marketing_target: Home and micro bakers selling at markets, online or from a small unit.
marketing_funnel: Free scaler/allergen label tool -> save recipes -> production planner and order list.
cold_outreach: Offer market-stall bakers a free allergen label sheet for their five best sellers in exchange for feedback.
post_ideas: I turned a bakery's Excel chaos into a bake-day plan: what I learned | Allergen labels for market stalls without paying for an ERP | Why scaling a sourdough formula by weight beats scaling by cups
competitors: Craftplan; Craftybase; Kitted; CrumbCounts
notes: Real demand (577-point Show HN) but an open-source competitor and several paid tools exist, so the wedge must be hosted simplicity plus the label/allergen dataset. Label rules differ by country; start with UK and EU allergens or one US state and state that it is not legal advice.

name: AirportRules
idea: Per-airport quick facts that general travel sites do not track: liquids limit status, exit-from-transit feasibility, left-luggage and bag-drop hours.
description: Each airport page shows whether the 100 ml liquids rule is still enforced (and which lanes use CT scanners), whether passengers can leave the departures or transit area, left-luggage and large-item storage options with hours, and earliest bag-drop time, each with a source link and verified date. Users can submit corrections. The moat is a hand-curated, dated, community-corrected dataset; the facts live on scattered airport pages and are only partly covered by news roundups.
why_hard_to_copy: Dated, sourced per-airport facts maintained by curation and user corrections; each fact must be verified at the airport's own page so it cannot be generated from a template.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel reading Supabase tables (airport, rule, source_url, verified_at); logged-in-free correction form with moderation queue.
satellite_what: One-page map and table of airports that have dropped the 100 ml limit, with last-verified dates.
marketing_where: FlyerTalk forums; TripAdvisor destination forums; Travel Stack Exchange (answer questions, link only where site rules allow); Facebook expat and digital-nomad groups; Show HN; Product Hunt; Travel and points-and-miles blogs (offer data as a link source)
marketing_target: Frequent flyers, families and layover travellers
marketing_funnel: Search 'does <airport> still have the 100ml rule' -> airport page.
cold_outreach: Pitch travel journalists who keep re-running 'which airports scrapped the liquids rule' lists with a live, dated source.
post_ideas: Which airports have scrapped the 100 ml rule right now (updated weekly) | Can you leave the airport on a layover? Airport-by-airport | Where to store a car seat or bike at 20 European airports
competitors: UK/Europe news roundups of airports that dropped the 100 ml rule; left-baggage.co.uk
notes: No dedicated tracker found in web search. Weakness: maintenance burden and staleness risk. Individual question view counts are 300-2,200, modest. Could be merged with NightTransfer if the coordinator wants a single airport-data product.

name: Relic
idea: Drag a dBase/FoxPro/Clipper/Paradox data file into the browser, browse it and export CSV/XLSX/SQLite without uploading anything.
description: Small firms still run DOS-era database apps whose data files nobody can open any more, and the people rescuing them hand-write parsers against format specs. Relic reads the common xBase variants (dBase III/IV, FoxPro/VFP, Clipper, memo files, DOS code pages, deleted-record flags) plus fixed-width text exports with a layout wizard, entirely client-side so business data never leaves the machine. Built for the consultant, relative or office manager who inherited the old system; the moat is breadth of format edge cases and a test corpus.
why_hard_to_copy: Parsing obscure legacy file formats correctly (memo blocks, code pages, packed numerics, variant headers) entirely client-side is exactly the long-tail work generic converters skip; the value compounds with every odd file added to the test corpus.
web_delivery: Static Next.js app on Vercel; parsing in a Web Worker with File API, export via client-side CSV/XLSX/SQLite-WASM; Supabase only for optional saved layouts and sample-file feedback.
satellite_what: Paste garbled accented text from an old file, detect CP437/850/852/1250/1252 mojibake and see the correct text.
marketing_where: Hacker News Show HN; Stack Overflow answers on .dbf questions; FoxPro/Clipper user forums such as Foxite; Small-business IT/MSP Facebook groups; Product Hunt
marketing_target: IT consultants, MSPs and relatives maintaining old business databases.
marketing_funnel: Free preview of the first rows (no upload) -> full export unlocked in browser; later saved layouts and batch conversion.
cold_outreach: Answer open 'how do I open this .dbf/.dat file' threads with a link and a sample conversion.
post_ideas: Show HN: I parse your 1989 dBase files in the browser, nothing uploaded | A field guide to the dBase/FoxPro/Clipper memo file mess | Rescuing a family business's data from a DOS box
competitors: DevToolLab DBF viewer; dbf2csv; LibreOffice Calc
notes: Strong repeated signal but willingness to pay is untested; commenters also say AI tools can now write one-off migrations, so the pitch is deterministic, private, no-upload parsing. A free tool with a donation or per-batch price fits the hobby tier.

name: OfficialEntry
idea: A hand-verified directory of the one official website for every ETA, e-visa and arrival card, with scam-lookalike warnings.
description: Travellers pick a destination and get the official government URL for its ETA, e-visa, digital arrival card or e-declaration, whether it is free or paid, who needs it, how early to file, and a last-verified date. A 'Is this site official?' check compares a pasted URL with the curated allowlist. The moat is the verified, dated dataset: several governments do not index their own portals, so scam resellers outrank them and nobody has a clean source of truth.
why_hard_to_copy: Hand-curated and dated registry of official portals (checked against embassy and ministry pages), plus a change log; scrapers cannot do it because many official portals are unindexed and the lookalike scam sites rank above them.
web_delivery: Static-first Next.js pages on Vercel Hobby (one SEO page per country and document) reading a Supabase table with source_url, official_domain, fee, verified_at; a 'report a change' form writes to Supabase.
satellite_what: Paste a URL and see whether it matches a verified government travel-document portal.
marketing_where: FlyerTalk forums; TripAdvisor destination forums; Travel Stack Exchange (answer questions, link only where site rules allow); Facebook expat and digital-nomad groups; Show HN; Product Hunt
marketing_target: First-time visitors to Southeast Asia, Gulf states and ETA countries; expats and travel-forum helpers
marketing_funnel: Search 'official <country> arrival card site' -> country page -> bookmark / share link.
cold_outreach: Email travel bloggers and immigration-advice forum moderators offering a verified link they can cite instead of ad-ridden pages.
post_ideas: The official MDAC / SGAC / Sri Lanka ETA links in one table (free, no fee) | How to spot a fake e-visa site in 10 seconds | Which countries now require a digital arrival card before landing
competitors: Sherpa entry-requirements checker (embedded in airline and agency sites); Smartraveller / news advisories on Bali arrival card scams
notes: Strongest multi-signal cluster in my data, but all signals come from one Q&A site (different askers). Low individual view counts on the official-site questions (157-569), higher on the general scam-site thread (1,324 views). SEO is uphill against scam and affiliate sites; ongoing verification effort is the real cost.

name: TicketName
idea: Show exactly how to type a long, multi-part or single name on an airline booking so it matches the passport.
description: User enters passport name parts and the airline; the tool outputs the first-name and last-name fields to use, handles field-length limits, single names (FNU/LNU conventions), suffixes, hyphens and missing middle names, and tells how risky the mismatch is. Includes a similar helper for two-field visa forms with Arabic and other multi-part names. The moat is a curated, airline-by-airline rules table; the logic has many edge cases that general advice pages skip.
why_hard_to_copy: Correctness-critical, hand-sourced airline and GDS name-field rules and edge-case logic (mononyms, double surnames, diacritics, length truncation) with citations to each carrier's own guidance.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel; rules in Supabase (airline, max_chars, single_name_format, suffix_rule, source_url); pure client-side formatter.
satellite_what: Type passport name and ticket name and see whether it is a safe, minor or risky mismatch.
marketing_where: FlyerTalk forums; TripAdvisor Air Travel forum; Travel Stack Exchange; Facebook groups for migrant workers and diaspora travel; Show HN
marketing_target: Travellers with long, single or multi-part names; travel agents
marketing_funnel: Search 'long name flight booking' -> tool page -> shortcut to airline guide.
cold_outreach: Offer travel agencies serving diaspora communities a free embeddable widget.
post_ideas: How to book a flight with a very long name: field limits by airline | Single-name passports: the FNU trick and when it fails | Missing middle name on your ticket: does it matter?
competitors: Air India passenger-name format policy; Finnair name elements guide; Trip.com passenger name guide
notes: No generator tool found in web search, only airline policy pages. Highest-engagement signal is the Arabic-name question (27 score, 2,781 views) but it is about a visa form, not a ticket. Rule data must be verified per airline; start with the top 30.

name: Plug-In Solar Rulebook
idea: Enter your country or US state and address: see whether plug-in (balcony) solar is allowed, the wattage cap, what to register, which devices qualify, and a realistic yield estimate.
description: Plug-in solar became legal or semi-legal in the UK, several US states and elsewhere during 2026, and every thread shows confusion: which certification applies, how many panels per circuit, what renters can do, what a US 120 V split-phase home means. The tool combines a hand-maintained rules table (caps, registration steps, certification such as UL 3700, circuit and socket limits, renter notes) with a free-data yield and payback estimate for the roof or balcony direction. The moat is the curated, constantly changing regulatory dataset plus honest uncertainty ranges, which generic solar calculators and one-country tools lack.
capital_note: Domain only; irradiance data from a free public API.
why_hard_to_copy: A hand-curated, dated rules dataset across jurisdictions that changed repeatedly in 2026, plus shading/orientation modelling and circuit-safety checks, needs domain research and upkeep that a quick vibe-coded calculator will not have.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel; rules stored as versioned rows in Supabase (with source links and last-verified dates); yield estimate calls a free public solar-irradiance API from a Vercel route with caching; static pages per country/state for search traffic.
satellite_name: Can I Plug It In Here?
satellite_what: A three-question checker (country/state, rented or owned, mounting) that returns a one-screen yes/maybe/no with the cap and the registration form to use.
marketing_where: Hacker News Show HN; Energy and solar forums (non-Reddit, e.g. DIY solar communities); Renter and apartment-living Facebook groups; Local sustainability newsletters; Mastodon and Bluesky energy communities
marketing_target: Renters and homeowners curious about plug-in solar, first in the UK and US states with new laws.
marketing_funnel: Free legality checker -> address yield estimate -> shopping and installation checklist.
cold_outreach: Share the checker with energy journalists and utility-advocacy groups covering new state laws.
post_ideas: Plug-in solar rules by state, kept current with sources | What 'G98' and 'UL 3700' mean for your balcony | How much will a vertical balcony panel really make where you live?
competitors: Helios; Balcony solar power (Wikipedia); Is balcony solar legal? country guide; pv magazine USA safety article; Octopus Energy plug-in solar
notes: Strong current attention (264-point thread, UK launch, US state laws) but the rules table is a maintenance commitment and must carry sources, last-verified dates and a clear 'not legal or electrical advice' notice. Affiliate or sales links should stay out to keep trust. Verify the terms of the chosen irradiance API before building.

name: BikeFit
idea: A bike-parts compatibility checker for standards, sizes and capacities.
description: User enters frame and drivetrain details and a target part; the tool checks bottom-bracket shell width and standard, cassette versus rear-derailleur capacity, chain length, tyre and rim width limits, and inch-versus-ETRTO tube sizes, and explains why. The moat is a curated cross-brand standards dataset with correctness-critical rules; manufacturers publish only their own parts.
why_hard_to_copy: Cross-brand standards dataset (BB shells, freehub splines, RD capacity, ETRTO) plus formula logic for chain length and clearance; needs cycling expertise.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel; component standards and rule tables in Supabase; checks client-side.
satellite_what: Convert inch, French and ETRTO sizes and show matching tube ranges.
marketing_where: Bicycles Stack Exchange; Bike forums (MTBR, Bike Forums); Facebook bike repair groups; Bike co-ops; Show HN
marketing_target: Home mechanics, bike co-op volunteers, used-bike restorers
marketing_funnel: Search 'will a 42t cassette fit my derailleur' -> tool.
cold_outreach: Offer bike co-ops a free printable compatibility card.
post_ideas: Will this cassette work with my rear derailleur? A 2-minute check | 68 vs 73 mm bottom bracket shells explained | 650B vs 27.5 vs 584: tyre size decoder
competitors: Shimano compatibility portal; Wolf Tooth parts finder; Competitive Cyclist compatibility hub
notes: Seven independent questions with moderate views (527-1,019). Mechanics data (BB standards, cassette limits) is mostly public but scattered. Not in my assigned niche list exactly, so niche chosen as Hobbies & Crafts.

name: Org Memory
idea: A handover binder for small volunteer-run organisations: policy review dates, officer terms, building maintenance records and renewals, with reminders and an audit log.
description: Small charities, churches and clubs lose records when the volunteer treasurer or retired admin leaves, and governance tools are priced for large boards. Org Memory keeps officer terms, policy review cycles, insurance and licence renewals, building inspections and invoices in one place, nudges the chair when a term or review is due, auto-fills meeting agendas and exports a handover pack. The moat is a curated, jurisdiction-specific governance and maintenance calendar (UK charity cycles first), not the file store.
why_hard_to_copy: The value is hand-curated governance calendars, policy templates and building-maintenance schedules by jurisdiction and building type, kept current by someone who knows the sector; a generic CRUD tracker lacks that.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel; Supabase Postgres with RLS and Storage for photos/PDFs (small files), email reminders via a free-tier email API on a scheduled function.
satellite_what: Free generator that lists the standard policies for a small charity or club with suggested review dates and downloads an ICS.
marketing_where: UK trustee and charity-admin communities; Church administrator forums; Small charity Facebook and LinkedIn groups; Hacker News
marketing_target: Chairs, secretaries and treasurers of small volunteer-run bodies.
marketing_funnel: Free policy calendar -> record store -> reminders and handover pack.
cold_outreach: Offer to pre-build a first-year governance calendar for a local charity as a pilot.
post_ideas: What happens when the volunteer treasurer leaves: a handover checklist | A one-page governance calendar for small charities | Why your church building needs a maintenance log
competitors: BoardPro; The Governance App (DSC); MyPlaceKeeper
notes: Deliberately excludes accounts, tax filings and donations (banned areas); it tracks dates and documents only. Present as organisational reminders, not legal or regulatory advice.

name: SafeCanning
idea: A canning planner that applies altitude, jar size and acidity rules to tested recipes and warns when a change makes it unsafe.
description: User picks a tested recipe family and altitude; the tool gives adjusted water-bath times or canner pressures, headspace and jar-size notes, and flags changes such as reduced sugar, added low-acid ingredients or process interruptions. It reproduces published USDA and extension tables and refuses to guess for untested changes. The moat is the careful, cited rules table and decision logic.
why_hard_to_copy: Correctness-critical, cited processing tables and 'is this change safe?' decision logic; hard to get right and not a weekend CRUD build.
web_delivery: Next.js PWA on Vercel; tables from public tested-recipe sources in Supabase; works offline in kitchens.
satellite_what: Simple altitude-to-extra-minutes table for water-bath canning with source links.
marketing_where: Canning and preserving Facebook groups; Extension service newsletters; Homesteading forums and blogs; YouTube canning channels; Show HN
marketing_target: Home canners, gardeners with seasonal gluts, homesteaders
marketing_funnel: Search 'canning altitude adjustment calculator' -> tool.
cold_outreach: Offer extension educators a link for handouts.
post_ideas: Altitude adjustment for water-bath canning in one table | Did you change the sugar? Is the jam still safe to can? | What to do when the canner pressure drops mid-process
competitors: UC Master Food Preserver altitude guidance; USU Utah altitude adjustments for home canning; National Center for Home Food Preservation
notes: Six different asks over the window. Strong liability angle: must stick to published tested values, show sources and tell users to discard when unsure. Several questions are 'is this safe?' rather than tool requests, so demand for a tool is inferred.

name: Fixture Glue
idea: Paste or upload a league's fixture list and get a subscribable calendar feed plus a weekly 'who can play?' poll for the team.
description: Amateur players and sports parents deal with leagues that each publish fixtures differently (web tables, PDFs, CSVs, printed sheets) and team chats that live elsewhere. Fixture Glue parses the common layouts client-side, normalises dates, times, venues and time zones, outputs a webcal feed that updates when a game moves, and gives the captain a one-click availability poll. The moat is a growing library of league-format parsers plus change detection.
why_hard_to_copy: The hard part is a messy-schedule parser library (odd date formats, multi-column PDFs, bye weeks, rescheduled games) and diffing updates, which accumulates league by league and is not a weekend job.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel; PDF text extraction with pdf.js and table heuristics run in the browser; ICS feed served from a Vercel route backed by Supabase; poll links need no login.
satellite_what: One-shot free converter: paste a fixture table or upload a PDF and download an ICS file.
marketing_where: Youth and amateur league Facebook groups; Local club WhatsApp groups via captains; Hacker News Show HN; Product Hunt; Parent-teacher and school sports newsletters
marketing_target: Team captains, coaches and sports parents in amateur leagues.
marketing_funnel: Free converter -> live feed -> availability poll for the whole team.
cold_outreach: Email league secretaries offering a free feed for their published schedule.
post_ideas: Turn any league PDF schedule into a calendar your whole family can subscribe to | Why league fixtures break your calendar import | The captain's Sunday-night availability poll, automated
competitors: smartcalendars.ai PDF to Calendar; PDF to Calendar Converter (iOS); Spond
notes: Two independent signals, one of them a developer musing about market size. Photo input would need OCR/vision (paid) and is left out of the core; text PDFs and web tables only.

name: Parenting Plan Calendar
idea: Free custody-schedule engine that turns a parenting-plan pattern plus holiday rules into one shared calendar and ICS feed.
description: Parents choose a base rotation (alternating weeks, 2-2-3, 5-2-2-5, custom) and then add holiday and school-break rules the way plans are actually written (even/odd years, first/second half of winter break, Friday-to-Monday weekends). The engine resolves rule precedence and outputs a color-coded year view, a printable PDF and a read-only ICS link for each parent's phone. Hard to copy because the value is the correctness of the rules engine and its holiday and school-calendar definitions, not the calendar UI.
why_hard_to_copy: Rule-precedence and holiday date algebra (odd/even years, split breaks, make-up days) is correctness-critical logic with many edge cases, plus a curated library of holiday and school-break definitions.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel; rules engine is pure TypeScript run in the browser; the schedule is saved as one Supabase row and served as an ICS route handler.
satellite_what: Free page: pick 2-2-3 or alternating weeks and see the whole year printed, with a basic holiday overlay.
marketing_where: Facebook co-parenting and single-parent groups; family mediators' and parenting-coordinator newsletters; Pinterest custody schedule boards; SEO pages for each named schedule pattern
marketing_target: Divorced or separated parents and mediators who need a clear year-long schedule
marketing_funnel: Free pattern page to saved shared schedule to optional paid add-ons for multiple children or school-district calendars
cold_outreach: Email family mediators with a free branded schedule printout to attach to parenting plans.
post_ideas: A year view of 2-2-3 vs 5-2-2-5 so you can see who has which holiday | How odd/even-year holiday rules actually resolve when they collide | Free ICS feed so both parents see the same exchange times
competitors: OurFamilyWizard Custody Schedule Builder; Custody X Change; 2houses; Cozi
notes: The TalkingParents complaint is about a court-mandated messaging product, which this idea does not replace (courts name the platform); the opening is the schedule piece and free tooling for parents who are not court-bound. Keep it a calendar, not legal advice; legal services are a banned niche so add a clear disclaimer and no document drafting. Pricing change dates for AppClose and TalkingParents in some comparison pages could not be verified, so only the Trustpilot reviews are used.

name: Camp Radar
idea: A hand-curated calendar of when local summer camp and class registrations open, with reminders ahead of each opening day.
description: Parents miss registration windows and end up taking whatever spots are left, because dates are scattered across town recreation pages and individual camp sites (resident-first windows, late-fee cutoffs and aid deadlines vary). Camp Radar starts with one metro area, hand-collects each provider's opening, resident-priority, late-fee and aid dates, and emails or exports ICS reminders per family. The moat is the curated dataset kept current, not the reminder code.
why_hard_to_copy: The defensible part is a hand-collected, locally verified registration-date dataset (and parent corrections), which takes sustained manual work per metro area.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel; Supabase table of providers/dates edited by an admin page; ICS export and email reminders from a scheduled function.
satellite_what: Paste a camp page link or enter an opening date, get an ICS reminder two weeks and one day before.
marketing_where: Local parent Facebook groups; School PTA newsletters; Neighbourhood email lists; Nextdoor-style community boards
marketing_target: Working parents of 5-12 year olds in one metro area.
marketing_funnel: Free reminder -> town-level calendar -> yearly sign-up for the next season.
cold_outreach: Send parent-group admins a free seasonal registration calendar for their town.
post_ideas: Every summer camp registration date for [town] in one page | Why camps fill in March and how to be ready | Resident-first registration windows explained
competitors: Town recreation registration pages; NeelCamp
notes: One signal and a seasonal product; the dataset work is the whole moat and must be done city by city. Do not offer auto-booking or payments (money area).

name: StitchTrack
idea: Browser-based tracker that reads a cross-stitch or knitting chart PDF and lets you tap off stitches and rows, offline.
description: Stitchers upload a born-digital pattern PDF; the app extracts the chart grid, symbols and thread legend in the browser, lets you mark completed stitches, highlight one thread colour, and count rows, saving progress locally and syncing to Supabase. It is aimed at people who buy PDF patterns from Etsy and pattern shops and are tired of subscription trackers and lost libraries. Hard to copy because reliable PDF chart parsing across pattern-maker layouts (symbol detection, legends, backstitch) is fiddly and needs a library of tested layouts.
why_hard_to_copy: Client-side extraction of symbol grids and legends from PDFs produced by many different pattern tools, plus thread-brand (DMC/Anchor) mapping, which needs a tested corpus of real patterns.
web_delivery: PWA on Vercel; pdf.js parses the PDF in the browser; chart image and progress live in IndexedDB, only small progress rows sync via Supabase.
satellite_what: Free page that tells a stitcher whether a purchased PDF will import cleanly and shows the extracted thread list.
marketing_where: Cross-stitch and knitting Facebook groups; Etsy pattern sellers (partner offer); Ravelry forums are login-gated so use a link in public blogs; Pinterest stitching boards
marketing_target: Cross-stitchers and knitters who buy PDF patterns and want a free cross-platform tracker
marketing_funnel: Free PDF checker, then free tracker for one active project, then paid for unlimited projects
cold_outreach: Offer Etsy pattern designers a compatibility report for their PDF layout in exchange for a link.
post_ideas: Which Etsy cross-stitch PDFs work with trackers and which do not | Track a 40,000-stitch chart on any device, no app store | Why my chart PDF failed to import: a checklist for pattern designers
competitors: Pattern Keeper; Purl: Pattern Tracker; StitchGrid; ClickStitch
notes: The market clearly exists (several iOS trackers launched in 2026) so this is a cross-platform web take, not an empty field; the signals are about paywalls, lost licences and PDF import, not an explicit request for a web version. Knitting charts are harder to parse than cross-stitch, so start with cross-stitch. Heavy PDFs must stay client-side to fit free storage.

name: RPG Shelf
idea: A catalog for tabletop RPG collectors that tracks print books, PDFs and backer rewards together, tagged by game system, edition and line.
description: TTRPG fans keep 1,000+ books across print shelves, DriveThruRPG, itch.io and crowdfunding, and today they juggle Google Sheets, PDF folders and BoardGameGeek's RPGGeek. RPG Shelf lets you add a book by cover, ISBN or product title, matches it to a canonical product (system, edition, line, format), and answers 'do I already own this?' from your phone at the game store. The moat is a curated TTRPG product taxonomy (system, edition, line, reprints, bundles) and a fix-it flow for items missing from public databases, which generic book trackers lack.
capital_note: Domain only; Open Library and browser barcode detection are free.
why_hard_to_copy: The value is a hand-curated RPG product database (system and edition mapping, reprints, bundle contents) plus user-contributed corrections; a generic book scanner clone does not know that a 5e core rulebook and its revised printing are one line.
web_delivery: Next.js PWA on Vercel hobby with Supabase Auth and Postgres; barcode lookup via the browser BarcodeDetector API with manual fallback; Open Library for ISBN metadata; offline cache so it works inside a game store.
satellite_what: Free page where you paste or upload your RPG Google Sheet or CSV and it matches titles to canonical products, flags duplicates and shows missing ISBNs.
marketing_where: RPG.net forums; EN World; RPGGeek guilds; TTRPG Discord servers; Kickstarter backer communities
marketing_target: TTRPG collectors with 300+ books and PDFs across several storefronts
marketing_funnel: Free sheet cleaner, then free tier up to 200 items, then paid unlimited if monetized later
cold_outreach: Reply to cataloging threads with a free shelf import for the thread's spreadsheet users.
post_ideas: I cleaned up a 1,600-book RPG spreadsheet automatically | Do you already own it? A phone check for the game store shelf | Why RPGGeek and BookWyrm both miss RPG editions
competitors: RPGGeek; COMPASS; Grimoire (ElfHosted); DriveThruRPG Library app; BookWyrm
notes: Single high-engagement thread, no older corroboration checked. BoardGameGeek XML API terms restrict commercial use and now need a token, so seed the product data from Open Library plus your own curation. Crowded adjacent space (book trackers), so the RPG-specific taxonomy must be the real differentiator.

name: OldRecordDecoder
idea: A searchable glossary and symbol guide for decoding old genealogy records: abbreviations, column codes, old scripts and register marks.
description: Users look up a record type and place (for example a UK 1939 Register annotation, a US church record index volume code, a Latin or French parish baptism entry, or Kurrent handwriting) and get a decoder with examples and links to sources. The moat is an expert-curated, cross-referenced glossary tied to record collections, built from genealogists' knowledge rather than generic dictionaries.
why_hard_to_copy: Expert-curated cross-collection glossary and example library; general OCR or AI transcription is unreliable for these scripts, so a reference people trust is the product.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel; glossary entries, example images (small, linked) and sources in Supabase.
satellite_what: Look up common annotations and strike-through meanings on the 1939 Register.
marketing_where: Genealogy Stack Exchange; Genealogy societies and mailing lists; FamilySearch Community; Facebook genealogy groups; Show HN
marketing_target: Family historians working with pre-1900 records
marketing_funnel: Search '<record type> abbreviations' -> glossary page.
cold_outreach: Offer genealogy societies a link for newsletters.
post_ideas: What the pencil marks on your 1939 Register entry mean | Latin words in Quebec baptism records | Common Kurrent letters that look alike
competitors: Transkribus Old German scripts; BYU German handwriting symbols and abbreviations; Polish Origins German records vocabulary
notes: Genealogy site volume is tiny (20 questions in the window) and views per question are 51-548, so demand evidence is modest. Moat depends on expert contributors; existing resources are fragmented, which is the gap.

name: LayoverCheck
idea: Estimate whether a tight connection or self-transfer is realistic at a specific airport, step by step.
description: User enters the arrival and departure terminals, ticket type (single vs separate), whether immigration and bag recheck are needed, and passport region; the tool lists each step (deplane, immigration, recheck, security, terminal change) with a typical time range and the bag-drop cutoff, and flags EES delays at Schengen airports. The moat is a hand-built per-airport process dataset for the busiest hubs, not generic minimum connection times.
why_hard_to_copy: Curated per-airport procedure data (terminal transfer routes, recheck and immigration rules, bag-drop closing times) that airlines do not publish for self-transfers.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel; per-airport step times and terminal-transfer notes in Supabase; calculation client-side.
marketing_where: FlyerTalk forums; TripAdvisor destination forums; Travel Stack Exchange (answer questions, link only where site rules allow); Facebook expat and digital-nomad groups; Show HN; Product Hunt; Cheap-flight and 'hacker fare' communities
marketing_target: Travellers booking self-transfers or short connections, especially long-haul with immigration
marketing_funnel: Search 'enough time to connect at <airport>' -> airport page -> checker.
cold_outreach: Message flight-deal bloggers who warn about self-transfers with a ready embed.
post_ideas: Is 45 minutes enough at O'Hare? A step-by-step budget | The 5 airports where a terminal change eats an hour | EES queues and your Schengen connection: how much buffer now?
competitors: CheckMyLayover; Eskimo travel MCT guide
notes: Competitor exists (CheckMyLayover). Seven separate threads in the window show recurring demand. Data creation for even 40 airports is manual; accuracy risk if times are wrong.

name: Open Slots Finder
idea: A filterable directory of artists and makers who currently have commission slots open, with price range, style and queue status.
description: Buyers of art, emotes, VTuber assets, game art and custom costumes currently hunt through social posts to find someone who is taking orders. This directory lets makers keep a profile (links to their own portfolio and own payment page, no money handled here) with a live open/closed/waitlist status, price bands and style tags, and lets buyers filter by type, budget and availability. Start with one tight vertical (for example Twitch/VTuber assets, or fursuit makers) so the list is complete and trusted before widening.
capital_note: Domain only; Supabase free and Vercel hobby cover 500 monthly users.
why_hard_to_copy: The code is easy; the moat is a hand-seeded, vetted maker list in one vertical and makers who keep their open/closed status fresh (network effect in a small niche). A clone with an empty directory is useless.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel hobby, Supabase Postgres + magic-link auth for makers to update their own status; profiles hold links and tiny thumbnails only, no image hosting.
satellite_name: Commission price and quote sheet generator
satellite_what: Free page where an artist fills in styles, prices and terms and gets a shareable price sheet / quote template.
marketing_where: Bluesky and X artist communities; Discord servers for VTuber/emote makers; Tumblr and Carrd link-lists; itch.io / gamedev Discords (for game artists); Product Hunt
marketing_target: Small digital artists and custom makers who want free visibility, and the buyers looking for them.
marketing_funnel: Maker sees the shared price sheet or a friend's profile, claims a free listing in two minutes, buyers find them by filter.
cold_outreach: DM 50 makers in one vertical offering to pre-fill their listing from their public pages, asking only for a yes.
post_ideas: Which emote artists have slots open this week (live list) | Free price sheet generator for commission artists | Price ranges for Twitch emote commissions, from listed profiles
competitors: Artists&Clients; ArtStation / Behance; Individual maker Carrd pages (queue/slot status per maker)
notes: Five independent X posts over six months, all asking the same thing in different verticals (I merged the fursuit maker request in as a first vertical). Honest weakness: marketplace cold start and existing generic platforms. No payments are held, only links out. The fursuit request is a single post.

name: Quorum
idea: Free-to-start voting and quorum tracking for HOAs, clubs and congregations, with ranked-choice tallying, proxies and a paper-ballot fallback.
description: Volunteer board members run an election once a year, worry that results can be challenged, and fear that members who do not use email get left out. Quorum handles member lists, one-person-one-ballot links, proxy and paper-ballot entry, live quorum tracking, several tally methods and a tamper-evident audit log. The moat is correct tally and quorum rules (single transferable vote, cumulative voting, proxy limits) and trust-building audit trails.
capital_note: Domain only; ballot emails stay inside a free email tier at small scale.
why_hard_to_copy: Tally algorithms (STV, cumulative, weighted votes), proxy/quorum rule engines, paper-ballot reconciliation and verifiable audit trails are correctness-critical and trust-critical, unlike a poll widget.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel; Supabase with RLS for ballots and a hash-chained audit table; ballot links by email through a free-tier email API (volume-limited).
satellite_what: Paste ballots and get STV/ranked-choice results with round-by-round counts.
marketing_where: HOA board member Facebook groups; Community association manager forums; Church and union admin communities; Hacker News
marketing_target: Volunteer board members who run annual elections.
marketing_funnel: Free tally calculator -> one-off election -> yearly subscription-free usage.
cold_outreach: Offer to run a small club's next officer election free as a case study.
post_ideas: How to run a defensible HOA election with volunteers | What quorum actually means in your bylaws, in plain language | Paper ballots plus online: reconciling both
competitors: Simply Voting; VotingPRO; Quick Vote Online; vote.direct
notes: One signal, crowded paid market, and elections carry reputational risk (must be clearly framed as a tool, not legal advice, and never handle dues or payments). Only worth it with strong audit-log design.

name: TransitCheck
idea: Tell a traveller whether a given passport needs a visa to transit a specific airport, airside or landside, single ticket or separate.
description: User enters passport nationality, any valid visas or residence permits, transit airport, and whether the legs are one ticket or self-transfer; the tool returns a verdict with the cited rule (Schengen airport transit visa lists, UK DATV, Canada transit, ETIAS airside exemption) and caveats. The moat is a sourced per-country rules table with last-verified dates, because the answer changes by nationality, visa held, ticket type and airport zone.
why_hard_to_copy: Correctness-critical rules engine over a hand-curated, cited dataset that changes often (nationality lists, exemptions for US/Schengen/UK visa holders); asking in forums is the current workaround because Timatic is paid.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel with a Supabase rules table (country, nationality group, exemption conditions, source URL, verified_at); evaluation runs in the browser.
marketing_where: FlyerTalk forums; TripAdvisor destination forums; Travel Stack Exchange (answer questions, link only where site rules allow); Facebook expat and digital-nomad groups; Show HN; Product Hunt; Expat and diaspora Facebook groups (Indian, Pakistani, Filipino travellers)
marketing_target: Passport holders from nationalities that face airport transit visas, and families booking connections
marketing_funnel: Search 'do I need a transit visa for <airport>' -> checker result -> share link in diaspora groups.
cold_outreach: Ask diaspora travel group admins to pin the tool; offer a free embed for travel agents.
post_ideas: Do you need a visa to change planes in Frankfurt? A passport-by-passport answer | Airside vs landside: why your hand baggage rules change the visa answer | Self-transfer in Schengen: the transit rule most people miss
competitors: MyTravelReady transit visa checker; Swiss FDFA airport transit visa page
notes: Direct competitor exists (MyTravelReady). Seven independent askers over 12 months is a good signal of recurring demand, but accuracy liability is real (must disclaim and cite sources). Consider merging with LayoverCheck if the coordinator wants fewer overlapping ideas.

name: Swiss Desk
idea: Run chess club nights and scholastic tournaments in the browser: Swiss pairings, standings, club ratings, results export, plus a scoresheet-repair tool.
description: Organisers currently juggle Google Forms for sign-up, desktop pairing software and text threads. Swiss Desk handles the roster, QR check-in, Swiss pairing with colour balance, byes and tiebreaks, a local club rating, a public standings link and a results export in the formats rating bodies expect. The builders on HN say matching real-world Swiss pairing rules is harder than it looks, which is the moat.
why_hard_to_copy: Swiss pairing rules (transpositions, colour alternation, floaters, forfeits, tiebreaks) and rating-report file formats are correctness-critical domain logic that a generic bracket builder gets wrong; one HN builder calls Swiss pairings 'more nuanced than they look'.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel, Supabase Postgres with Realtime for live standings; pairing engine in TypeScript runs client-side and is unit-tested against known tournaments.
satellite_what: Paste handwritten-score-sheet moves; the tool finds the first illegal or ambiguous move, suggests fixes and keeps the rest of the game.
marketing_where: TalkChess and Lichess forums; Scholastic chess coach Facebook groups; US Chess and national federation organiser forums; Hacker News Show HN; Chess club newsletters
marketing_target: Chess club organisers and scholastic tournament directors.
marketing_funnel: Free scoresheet fixer -> club roster -> run a club night -> run a rated tournament.
cold_outreach: Offer to run one club's next event free in exchange for a pairing audit against their current software.
post_ideas: Why Swiss pairing is harder than it looks (with test cases) | Run your school chess tournament from a phone | Fixing the moves your kid mis-wrote on the scoresheet
competitors: SwissSys; Chess Host; SWIPS; OpenChessClub
notes: Crowded: free browser tools already exist, so this only works if pairing correctness and rating-report exports clearly beat them. Do not take entry fees or payments (banned money area).

name: Field Checklist
idea: Offline-first birding checklist logger that never loses unsubmitted lists and exports eBird-ready CSV.
description: Birders log species counts, location, time and protocol in the field with no signal, using an offline taxonomy of species names and codes; lists stay on the device and sync when online, and a validated CSV in eBird's import layout is generated so nothing is retyped. Birders can start a list for any place, not just near their GPS fix, and edit past lists in bulk. Hard to copy because of the offline taxonomy handling, protocol and date/location validation rules that eBird's importer enforces, and loss-proof offline-first storage.
capital_note: Domain name only; eBird API key is free but optional.
why_hard_to_copy: Offline-first storage that cannot lose lists, plus a maintained taxonomy and importer-validation rule set; the eBird CSV format has strict requirements (one date, one location, a protocol per list).
web_delivery: PWA on Vercel with a service worker and IndexedDB; taxonomy as a static JSON pack; optional Supabase sync; CSV generated in the browser for eBird's web import tool.
satellite_what: Free page that validates a CSV against eBird's import rules and flags errors before upload.
marketing_where: BirdForum and local Audubon chapter newsletters; regional birding mailing lists and Facebook groups; big-year and Christmas Bird Count organisers; Product Hunt
marketing_target: Birders who bird in places without reception (backcountry, islands, boats)
marketing_funnel: Free CSV checker to free offline logger to optional sync and backup
cold_outreach: Email Christmas Bird Count compilers offering a ready-to-upload CSV workflow for volunteers without data service.
post_ideas: I lost 100 unsubmitted checklists: how I log birds with no signal now | Why eBird rejects your CSV and how to fix it before uploading | Start a checklist anywhere: logging yesterday's birds from your couch
competitors: eBird (official app); Birda; Birdathon; eBird bulk import rules; eBird Mobile; Birdathon (iOS)
notes: Only a handful of recent low-star reviews, and the incumbent app is free and loved by most users (high rating), so the opening is narrow: offline loss-proofing and custom location. iOS Safari PWA storage can be evicted so export and sync must be prominent. eBird says bulk upload should not be the main entry method; check terms before promoting this route.

name: Lingua Reader
idea: Browser reader for language learners: click any word for a dictionary entry, track known words, no forced AI and no per-month wall.
description: Learners paste or import articles, EPUBs and subtitle files, and the app splits them into words (including Japanese, Chinese and Thai with browser-native segmentation), colours each word by how well you know it, and shows an offline dictionary entry on click. Known-word counts, lemma handling and an Anki-ready export are built in, and a text's vocabulary coverage is shown before you start reading. It targets people leaving LingQ-style paid readers over mandatory AI features and instability. Hard to copy because tokenisation, lemmatisation across inflections and the bundled open dictionaries (Wiktionary, JMdict, CC-CEDICT) are language-by-language data and NLP work.
capital_note: Domain name only; dictionary data is open-licensed and ships as static files.
why_hard_to_copy: Per-language segmentation, lemmatisation and dictionary pipelines (CJK, Thai, inflected European languages) plus accurate known-word tracking across word forms; a flashcard clone is easy, this is not.
web_delivery: Next.js PWA on Vercel; dictionaries and segmentation data shipped as per-language packs cached in IndexedDB; word-status rows synced through Supabase.
satellite_what: Free page: paste any article and see how many of its words fall in the top 1,000/3,000/5,000 for the language, with an unknown-word list.
marketing_where: language-learning forums such as HTLAL and learner Discords; Japanese, Chinese and Korean study communities; Anki forum shares; Product Hunt and Show HN
marketing_target: Intermediate learners who read native texts and want free tooling with no AI
marketing_funnel: Free coverage checker, then free reader with 3 languages, then paid for large libraries, audio sync and cloud backup
cold_outreach: Message polyglot YouTubers and bloggers who review LingQ with a free account and a language pack they care about.
post_ideas: Read your first novel in Japanese with a free offline dictionary, no AI | How many words do you actually need to read this article? A coverage checker | Leaving LingQ: what I wish a reader app did differently
competitors: Lute; LWT (Learning with Texts); Readlang; LingQ
notes: Three independent LingQ reviews describe different gaps within two months, but no review explicitly asks for a web tool; Lute and LWT already serve self-hosters, so the angle is a hosted, no-install, no-AI reader. Data licensing needs checking (Wiktionary CC BY-SA, JMdict EDRDG licence). Each added language is real linguistic work.

name: Hosted Reading Sync (KOReader-compatible)
idea: A free hosted progress-sync endpoint for KOReader e-reader users plus a browser dashboard of reading stats, so nobody has to self-host a sync server.
description: Gives each reader a personal sync account whose address they paste into KOReader; progress per book is stored as tiny rows and shown on a web dashboard. Users can also drop their KOReader statistics file into the page and get charts computed entirely in the browser. Aimed at e-ink readers who want position sync across devices without Docker. Hard to copy because the sync protocol has device/document-hash quirks and the stats file is an obscure SQLite schema.
capital_note: Domain name; Supabase and Vercel free tiers cover the small rows.
why_hard_to_copy: Needs wire-compatibility with an existing device-side protocol (document hashing, never-sync-backwards rules) and parsing of KOReader's statistics database client-side; niche e-reader knowledge most vibe coders lack.
web_delivery: Vercel serverless routes implement the sync HTTP API against Supabase Postgres (one small row per user+book); dashboard is a normal web app; statistics.sqlite is parsed client-side with sql.js (WASM). No file storage needed.
satellite_what: Free page where you drop your KOReader statistics file and get reading charts (pages per day, time per book, streaks) computed locally.
marketing_where: MobileRead forums; KOReader GitHub discussions; Hacker News Show HN; AlternativeTo listing; e-reader Discord servers
marketing_target: KOReader users on Kindle, Kobo, Pocketbook and Android who do not run a home server
marketing_funnel: Stats viewer page -> create free sync account -> paste address into KOReader
cold_outreach: Reply helpfully on sync-failure threads and offer the hosted endpoint as a fallback.
post_ideas: I made a free place to sync KOReader progress without Docker | Drop your statistics file here and see your reading year in charts | What happens to your progress when the default sync server is down?
competitors: KoInsight; koreader-driftless; korrosync
notes: Demand evidence is spread over several projects and mostly older threads that stay active; the KOReader outage thread is a single event. Self-hosted alternatives exist, so the pitch is purely 'no server to run'. I did not verify the exact sync API surface in this session.

name: MiterReach
idea: Check whether a given mitre saw can make a specific cut, including angled cuts and flip cuts.
description: User enters the saw model (or blade size and slide travel) and the board profile and angles; the tool shows the maximum crosscut and height at that miter and bevel, whether a flip cut works, and the clearance needed. The moat is a hand-collected saw-capacity table from manuals plus geometry, which published 'max cut' specs hide.
why_hard_to_copy: Per-model capacity data at angles (mostly in PDF manuals) combined with cut geometry; buyers cannot get this from spec sheets that quote only 0-degree capacity.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel; saw specs in Supabase; geometry rendered client-side as a 2D diagram.
marketing_where: Woodworking forums; Tool-review blogs; Facebook DIY groups; YouTube tool channels; Show HN
marketing_target: Buyers choosing a mitre saw; DIY carpenters
marketing_funnel: Search 'can my miter saw cut a 2x12' -> tool.
cold_outreach: Offer tool-review blogs a capacity widget per model.
post_ideas: Can a 10-inch mitre saw cut a 2x6 at 56 degrees? | Flip cuts: how wide a board you can really cut | Saw capacity cheat sheet by model
competitors: Omni Calculator miter angle
notes: Two signals, low-moderate views (744 and 1,109) and a niche audience. Included because the moat (curated per-model data) is real but demand is thin; likely better as a feature of a larger tool-buying site.

name: SowRight
idea: Garden planner that gets planting dates right: local frost dates, crop-specific rules and succession planting, with no subscription.
description: Gardeners enter a location and bed layout; the planner uses frost-date normals and a hand-checked crop rules table (days to maturity, soil-temperature limits, direct sow vs transplant, succession intervals) to generate a dated sow, transplant and harvest calendar that updates as crops are harvested. It is for home vegetable growers who have caught consumer garden apps giving wrong advice or locking basics behind subscriptions. Hard to copy because the value is an expert-verified, region-aware crop dataset and scheduling logic, not the UI.
capital_note: Domain name only; frost data comes from a public dataset.
why_hard_to_copy: A curated and verified crop-rules dataset by climate and frost date plus succession and harvest-date logic; generic AI-generated advice is the exact failure reviewers describe.
web_delivery: Next.js PWA on Vercel; crop rules and frost-date data are static JSON (public NOAA-style normals); user beds and plantings in Supabase.
satellite_what: Free page: enter ZIP/postcode and get frost dates plus a one-page sow calendar for common crops.
marketing_where: Extension master-gardener newsletters and local garden club groups; Houzz and other gardening forums; regional Facebook gardening groups by zone; seed company newsletters
marketing_target: Home vegetable gardeners in cool-season climates with short frost windows
marketing_funnel: Free frost-date page, then free planner for one bed set, then paid for multiple gardens and printable plans
cold_outreach: Offer master gardener programs a free zone-specific planting calendar printout.
post_ideas: Why your garden app told you to start squash indoors too early | Succession planting dates for lettuce by last-frost date | Free frost-date lookup with a sow calendar
competitors: Seed to Spoon; Planter; GrowIt; NParks Sowing and Harvest Planner
notes: Planting-rule accuracy is only as good as the dataset; building and verifying it for even 60 crops across climates is real expert work and the biggest cost (time, not cash). Free web calendars exist in some regions (e.g., Singapore NParks), so differentiation is accuracy plus succession and bed tracking.

name: Mail Vault Viewer
idea: Open, search and convert old mailbox archives (mbox, EML folders, PST) locally in the browser without importing them into a mail client.
description: Drop a big mbox, a folder of .eml files or an Outlook PST and get a searchable threaded view with attachments, plus export to a stable format (EML + index, PDF per thread). Aimed at people archiving decades of mail or reviewing exported evidence. Moat is streaming huge mailboxes client-side, MIME and charset edge cases, and PST parsing.
why_hard_to_copy: Robust parsing of multi-GB mbox and PST files with broken MIME, odd charsets and nested attachments in memory-limited browsers is hard; but an mbox web viewer already exists, so the PST/EML-folder breadth is the differentiator.
web_delivery: Static web app on Vercel; Web Worker streaming parser with a SQLite-wasm/IndexedDB search index; nothing uploaded.
marketing_where: Hacker News Show HN; Lemmy c/selfhosted; Digital archivist communities (ePADD, Mailbagit users); Genealogy and family-history forums
marketing_target: People holding old mailboxes, family archivists, small-firm admins with exported mail.
marketing_funnel: Free viewer for files up to a size cap -> unlock for big archives and exports.
cold_outreach: Answer 'how do I read an mbox file' questions.
post_ideas: Open a 10 GB mbox in a browser tab without uploading | Archive 25 years of email in formats that will not die | Read PST files without Outlook
competitors: Mboxreader; Thunderbird
notes: An mbox-in-browser competitor already exists, so only PST/EML-folder breadth and big-file performance would distinguish it. PST parsing in JS libraries is less mature.

name: PubOpen
idea: Open and convert old Microsoft Publisher .pub files to PDF, SVG or editable text entirely in the browser.
description: Microsoft Publisher stopped being part of Microsoft 365 on 1 October 2026, so offices, schools and clubs are left with years of .pub newsletters, flyers and labels they can no longer edit. This tool parses the legacy .pub container in the browser (nothing is uploaded) and exports a PDF, page images and the extracted text and fonts for rebuilding in Word or Canva. Hard to copy because .pub is an obscure reverse-engineered binary format and good fidelity needs a WebAssembly build of an existing parser plus lots of real-world test files.
capital_note: Domain name only; WASM bundle fits Vercel static hosting.
why_hard_to_copy: Parsing a proprietary legacy binary format client-side with decent layout fidelity; the work is porting a C++ library to WASM and tuning it against a corpus of real .pub files.
web_delivery: Static site on Vercel; the parser (libmspub compiled to WebAssembly) runs fully client-side, so there is no server cost and no file upload.
satellite_what: Free page that shows page count, embedded fonts and linked images of a .pub without uploading it.
marketing_where: IT-admin communities and school district tech forums; Microsoft 365 admin blogs and newsletters; church office and nonprofit admin Facebook groups; Hacker News Show HN
marketing_target: Small offices, schools, churches and clubs with legacy Publisher files and no Publisher licence
marketing_funnel: Free client-side converter, then paid batch folder conversion for IT admins
cold_outreach: Pitch IT help-desk pages (like the university notices) to add a no-upload converter link to their Publisher retirement guides.
post_ideas: Convert .pub files without Publisher or uploading them anywhere | What you lose when you export a Publisher newsletter to PDF | Inventory every .pub on your drive before the deadline
competitors: LibreOffice Draw; Microsoft PowerShell bulk converter
notes: Demand evidence is institutional notices, not end users complaining; I did not find a user thread. Build risk is high: porting libmspub to WASM and getting acceptable fidelity may take weeks, and LibreOffice already opens .pub on desktop. Date on the second source is the page's own 'last updated' stamp.

name: PreRead
idea: Drop in an EPUB and get the unknown words (after subtracting words you already know) ranked by frequency, with context sentences and Anki export, all in the browser.
description: Language learners who read books want to learn a text's vocabulary before reading it: lemmatise every word, count occurrences, filter out known words, attach a bilingual definition and the original sentence, and export flashcards. PreRead does it client-side so copyrighted books never leave the device, and can also rank a library of EPUBs by lexical difficulty (unique-word count). Moat is per-language lemmatisation and inflection data plus a known-words model that persists across books.
capital_note: Domain name only; Supabase free + Vercel hobby cover hosting
why_hard_to_copy: Needs per-language lemma/inflection data and clean handling of elisions, multiword expressions and proper nouns; a generic LLM wrapper cannot do deterministic frequency counts over a whole book.
web_delivery: EPUB unzip + tokenise + lemma lookup entirely in the browser (Web Worker, open lemma lists); known-word list and settings synced via Supabase; static data files on Vercel.
satellite_what: Drop an EPUB and see unique-word count, estimated coverage of the top 2000 words and a rough difficulty band.
marketing_where: Lemmy c/languagelearning; Language-specific forums; Anki forums; Learner YouTube comment sections
marketing_target: Intermediate learners reading real books in French, Spanish, German, Italian
marketing_funnel: Difficulty meter -> unknown-word list -> account for known-word sync
cold_outreach: Reply to learners posting about extracting word lists by hand
post_ideas: I ranked 600 French EPUBs by vocabulary difficulty | Learn a book's words before you read it: workflow | Graded readers vs frequency-ranked prereading
competitors: JPDB; Jihanzi; han-cihui; TeakReader
notes: Existing tools are single-language or CLI; a general multi-language web version looks open. Lemma data coverage per language is the real work; start with French or Spanish.

name: Open When
idea: A family binder that tells loved ones where everything is and what to do with each online account after you die or are incapacitated, without storing passwords.
description: People worry about what a spouse would face with email, photo storage, subscriptions and documents after a death, and a password manager alone does not explain what to do. Open When keeps an inventory of accounts by provider with the exact memorialise/close/transfer steps, who the family contact is and where documents live, encrypted in the browser and released to named people only on a check-in lapse or manual trigger. The moat is a curated, regularly updated per-provider procedures dataset plus careful client-side encryption.
why_hard_to_copy: The provider-by-provider procedures dataset (Apple, Google, Meta, banks' notification steps etc.) must be researched and kept current, and zero-knowledge encryption plus a safe release flow is easy to get wrong.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel; client-side encryption (Web Crypto) before data reaches Supabase; scheduled function sends a check-in email and releases a sealed link to trusted contacts if unanswered.
satellite_what: A printable checklist generator that lists the accounts most people forget, with memorialise/close links per provider.
marketing_where: Personal-finance-adjacent blogs (non-advice angle); Hospice and caregiver support communities; Password-manager user forums; Hacker News
marketing_target: Adults 35-65 with a spouse or ageing parents and many online accounts.
marketing_funnel: Free checklist -> encrypted binder -> trusted-contact release.
cold_outreach: Offer family-support nonprofits a branded checklist for their workshops.
post_ideas: What your family needs to do with your Google and Apple accounts | The digital legacy checklist nobody gives you | Why 'give them my password manager' is not a plan
competitors: Apple Legacy Contact / Google Inactive Account Manager; Planning checklists (insurers, estate lawyers); Seal (iOS)
notes: One signal; trust and liability (data loss, wrongful release) are significant. Do not store account passwords or financial data; keep to locations and instructions, and avoid legal/estate advice. The trusted-contact release flow adds a scheduled email job (Supabase cron on the free plan is enough). A second builder (Seal, Sep 2026) shows others see the same need; the open design question from that thread is who decides someone is gone and how to avoid false triggers.

name: GedFix
idea: Client-side GEDCOM checker and upgrader that reads messy 5.5.1 exports and produces clean GEDCOM 7 without uploading the family tree anywhere.
description: Genealogists paste or drop a .ged file and get a report of structural problems, a plain-language fix list, and a converted GEDCOM 7 file, all inside the browser so private family data never leaves the device. Targets exports from Family Tree Maker, RootsMagic, Ancestry and others, which each bend the standard differently. Hard to copy because correctness depends on many vendor quirks and the GEDCOM 7 spec.
why_hard_to_copy: Vendor-specific export quirks and GEDCOM 7 edge cases (extensions, EXID, GEDZIP) must be handled correctly entirely client-side.
web_delivery: Static web app with a parser running in a Web Worker; Supabase only for optional saved fix-profiles.
satellite_what: Browser tool that strips living people and notes from a GEDCOM before sharing.
marketing_where: RootsChat; Gramps Discourse; WikiTree G2G; Genealogy Facebook groups
marketing_target: Hobby genealogists switching tree software
marketing_funnel: Free validator report -> one-click fix -> GEDCOM 7 download
cold_outreach: Reply to people posting import errors with a link that diagnoses the exact file.
post_ideas: Why your GEDCOM will not import and how to fix it | GEDCOM 7 in plain English | Move your tree between programs without losing sources
competitors: GEDminer GEDCOM validator; GED-inline; gedcom.io converter list
notes: Signals are scattered GitHub issues in different tools, not direct requests for a standalone fixer. Several free validators/converters already exist, so the moat is quality of vendor-quirk handling, not a new category.

name: Volunteer Rota
idea: A volunteer and club rota builder that fills shifts automatically from people's availability and handles swaps and find-a-sub requests.
description: Organisers list roles and dates, volunteers mark when they cannot serve, and the tool proposes a fair rota; volunteers accept, decline or ask for a substitute from a simple link, no app install. Aimed at small churches, clubs, food banks and school groups that outgrew spreadsheets. The moat is the fairness-aware auto-fill logic with constraints, which is real scheduling logic rather than CRUD.
why_hard_to_copy: Constraint scheduling (availability, blackout dates, fairness, team balance) and swap workflows are correctness-critical, unlike a simple signup sheet.
web_delivery: Web app on Vercel with Supabase; constraint-based auto-fill runs in the browser or a serverless function; magic-link responses and calendar feed per volunteer.
satellite_what: Paste a rota spreadsheet and see who is overloaded and who is never scheduled.
marketing_where: church and ministry leader communities; school PTA groups; food bank coordinator networks; Product Hunt; AlternativeTo
marketing_target: Volunteer coordinators at small churches, clubs and food banks
marketing_funnel: Fairness checker -> import volunteers -> auto-fill rota
cold_outreach: Email coordinators of local organisations with a free first rota.
post_ideas: Stop being the person who texts everyone to find a sub | Is your volunteer rota fair? Check it in 30 seconds | Auto-fill a month of shifts around people's blackout dates
competitors: RosterThat; WhenToHelp; Shifts by Everhour; SignUpGenius
notes: Crowded niche with free tiers. GitHub evidence is weak (a single project roadmap). Included for niche coverage; any donation/contribution handling is deliberately out of scope.

name: OpenLoop Pattern Finder
idea: Free, AI-free search engine for crochet and knit patterns that links out to designers' own sites and filters properly.
description: People are leaving 1-3 star reviews on pattern apps because almost everything sits behind a Pro paywall, the photos look AI-generated, and there is no real search or free-only filter. This is a PWA index of free, human-made patterns (title, thumbnail link, yarn weight, hook/needle size, skill level, item type, time) that always sends the visitor to the designer's own page so ads and affiliate links are preserved. Moat: a hand-curated, normalised pattern dataset (yarn-weight and gauge normalisation, dedup across sites) and designer-friendly link-out, which scraper apps are being blamed for ignoring.
capital_note: Domain only; Supabase free and Vercel hobby cover the index.
why_hard_to_copy: The value is the curated, de-duplicated and normalised free-pattern index with designer opt-in; the code is easy but the dataset and designer trust take months of manual work.
