description: Pick a font you are replacing; the tool ranks open-licensed fonts by visual similarity (weight, width, x-height, stroke contrast) and script coverage, shows each license with a link to the license file, and previews your own text. Built for game and app makers hit by font license price hikes. Moat is a hand-curated, license-checked dataset of open CJK and Latin fonts with measured metrics.
why_hard_to_copy: Needs a curated, verified dataset of open font licenses and glyph coverage (CJK variants are messy) plus similarity metrics; a prompt-built version would lack trustworthy data. Must not be presented as legal advice.
web_delivery: Static site on Vercel; font metrics and licence records as JSON; client-side preview using web fonts; Supabase optional for user submissions.
satellite_what: Paste a font name and see its license family and a link to the license file (not legal advice).
marketing_where: Game dev Discords and Mastodon; Hacker News Show HN; itch.io devlogs; Typography communities; Lemmy gamedev communities
marketing_target: Indie game and app developers who ship text in CJK languages and need license certainty.
marketing_funnel: Free license check -> free look-alike finder -> saved shortlists.
cold_outreach: Reply to font-license price-hike news with a shortlist tool for affected studios.
post_ideas: Open-license replacements for popular Japanese UI fonts | How to check a CJK font's glyph coverage before shipping | Font license changed overnight: a survival checklist
competitors: Wikipedia list of CJK fonts; IBM Plex Sans JP coverage article
notes: Only one thread; hard-to-copy part is a data curation effort that is large. Legal risk if users treat results as license advice, so keep to linking primary license files. Skews to game developers, a niche.

name: Exam Pseudocode Studio
idea: Browser IDE that runs AQA/OCR/Cambridge/IB exam pseudocode, fills the trace table automatically and draws the matching flowchart from the same code.
description: Students and teachers write pseudocode in the exact dialect of their exam board, step through it, and get a trace table generated as it runs plus a flowchart rendered from the same program, so all three exam representations stay consistent. Teachers can share exercises by link. Hard to copy because it needs dialect-accurate parsers and an interpreter for several boards' pseudocode specifications and a flowchart layout that follows exam conventions.
why_hard_to_copy: Exam-board-specific pseudocode dialects with exact semantics (arrays indexing, string functions, file handling) and exam-style flowchart and trace-table conventions; niche syllabus knowledge most developers lack.
web_delivery: Static SPA on Vercel hobby; parser/interpreter and flowchart layout run in the browser (web worker); Supabase free for shared exercises and class codes.
satellite_what: Paste a short loop in plain pseudocode and get a printable trace table for homework or revision.
marketing_where: Computing At School (CAS) community; TES resources marketplace; Isaac Computer Science teacher community; Teacher Facebook and Discord groups for GCSE/IGCSE computing
marketing_target: GCSE, IGCSE and A-level computer science teachers and students
marketing_funnel: Free trace table page -> Studio -> teacher shares class exercise links before exams
cold_outreach: Email CS department heads offering a ready set of past-paper-style exercises that run in the tool.
post_ideas: Auto trace tables for AQA pseudocode (free) | Draw the flowchart from your pseudocode - for OCR J277 revision | Why your trace table loses marks and how to check it
competitors: Coddy exam pseudocode editors; PseudoRun (Firefox extension); Pseudocoder (Chrome extension)
notes: One true user request plus a builder signal. Existing browser runners already cover editing and running, so the differentiator is the flowchart plus trace table in one place and board-accurate dialects. Teachers adopt tools slowly; seasonal around exam dates.

name: ALPR Incident Ledger
idea: A sourced ledger of documented license-plate-reader misuse cases and documented solved cases by city.
description: People on opposite sides of the debate want an aggregation of documented Flock camera incidents: one wants misuse by police compiled, another wants a list of crimes the cameras deterred or solved. A ledger with citations, dates and public-records links per city would serve both, separated from the camera location maps that already exist.
why_hard_to_copy: Editorial rigor: each entry needs a primary source and consistent classification, which takes sustained curation; local public-records requests make it better over time.
web_delivery: Next.js + Supabase table of incidents with source URLs; editor workflow for submissions; static pages per city.
marketing_where: Civil liberties groups and local government watchdog communities; Local news outlets; Mastodon and Bluesky privacy circles
marketing_target: Residents, journalists and council staff researching ALPR contracts.
marketing_funnel: City pages in search, then submissions.
cold_outreach: Offer the ledger to reporters covering a local contract vote.
post_ideas: Every documented misuse case in one state with sources | What the city audit logs actually showed
competitors: DeFlock; Local news how-to guides on finding Flock cameras
notes: Politically charged; legal and defamation risk if sourcing is weak, so every row must cite a primary source. Two posts from opposite sides give a fair demand signal.

name: ChartWright
idea: Knitting and crochet chart editor in the browser whose written instructions are correct for flat versus in-the-round work.
description: A paying knitting-chart app user says the written instructions come out wrong when switching a chart from flat to in the round (rows read left to right while the knits and purls are not reversed); another says large colourwork charts such as corner-to-corner are painful because zooming and panning draw random cells. ChartWright is a canvas chart editor with a stitch-symbol grammar that converts charts to written lines and back, handles right-side/wrong-side reversal, repeats and stitch-count changes, and works with a stylus or mouse with proper pan/zoom. Moat is the domain logic.
why_hard_to_copy: Correctness-critical stitch grammar (RS/WS reversal, in-the-round, repeats, increases/decreases changing counts) plus a large-chart editor; knitters will spot errors immediately.
web_delivery: Canvas/SVG editor as a PWA on Vercel; charts stored as JSON in Supabase; PNG/PDF export client-side.
satellite_name: Chart reading direction explainer and converter
satellite_what: Paste a one-sided chart or written row and get the opposite-side row and in-the-round version.
marketing_where: knitting designer newsletters and Instagram; Pinterest knitting boards; Ravelry forums (read-only research, post only if allowed); Facebook pattern-designer groups
marketing_target: Independent knit and crochet pattern designers and chart-following hobbyists.
marketing_funnel: Free flat/round converter -> editor -> export to PDF for sale.
cold_outreach: Offer indie designers a free test of exporting chart plus written instructions that match.
post_ideas: Why your written instructions disagree with your chart in the round | Draw a big C2C chart without random cells | Free RS/WS row converter
competitors: Stitch Fiddle; Knitting Chart (iOS)
notes: Only three reviews of one small app (rc about 1.3k), Stitch Fiddle already exists. Kept because the domain-logic moat is real; verify demand before building.

name: Sideline Story
idea: Volunteer-friendly web scoreboard for school sports broadcasts that turns the game log into runs, streaks and talking points for student commentators.
description: Community groups that livestream local high school games struggle with clunky scoreboard software that is hard to learn. This tool lets any teenager with a tablet keep the score and automatically surfaces scoring runs, lead changes and streak facts on a stream overlay for commentators to read. The moat is sport-specific event models and storyline detection rather than the scoreboard itself.
why_hard_to_copy: Realtime sync plus sport-specific play-log models (runs, streaks, momentum, lead changes per sport) is real domain logic; the scoreboard UI alone is easy.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel; the scorer's tablet writes events to Supabase Realtime; an OBS browser-source URL renders the overlay and live charts.
satellite_what: Pick a sport and colours and get an OBS browser-source scorebug URL in a minute.
marketing_where: OBS forum and Discord communities; High school AV/broadcast club forums; NFHS-style school streaming Facebook groups; Hacker News Show HN
marketing_target: Volunteer broadcasters, school AV clubs and parent streamers.
marketing_funnel: Free scorebug -> scorekeeping tablet UI -> storyline panel.
cold_outreach: Message school broadcast clubs with a ready overlay in their colours.
post_ideas: Let a 12-year-old run the scoreboard: lessons from streaming school games | From play log to talking points: runs and streaks detection | A free OBS scorebug in your team colours
competitors: KeepTheScore; ScoreLeader
notes: Single signal and free competitors exist; the differentiator is the storyline layer. Start with one sport (basketball) to keep the log model small.

name: Luck Tuner
idea: Interactive designer for fair-feeling randomness: compare plain chance, pity counters, pseudo-random distribution and shuffle bags, and get exact streak statistics and code.
description: A game designer enters a target drop or crit chance and sees side by side how independent rolls, pity timers, increasing-chance (PRD) and shuffle-bag systems behave: longest failure streak, expected attempts, variance, and a tunable knob between fully random and fully predictable. The tool solves the constants numerically and exports snippets for common engines. Aimed at indie developers and tabletop designers. Hard to copy because it needs exact Markov-chain analysis and numeric constant solving rather than Monte Carlo guesses.
why_hard_to_copy: Exact Markov-chain streak distributions and numeric PRD constant solving across several systems, with clear visualisation; most posts only hand-wave the math.
web_delivery: Static SPA on Vercel hobby; analysis and simulation in a web worker; shareable parameter links; no backend needed.
satellite_what: Static table and mini-calculator: nominal chance in, PRD constant and first-hit chance out.
marketing_where: Game Development Stack Exchange answers; Roblox DevForum; itch.io devlog communities; Godot and Unity community forums
marketing_target: Indie game developers and gacha or loot designers
marketing_funnel: Constant lookup page -> streak visualizer -> code export
cold_outreach: Reply to forum threads about RNG feeling unfair with a one-link demo of the streak comparison.
post_ideas: Why a 25% crit still gives 12-hit dry streaks and how PRD fixes it | Pity timer vs shuffle bag: exact streak numbers | Tune your loot luck without a spreadsheet
competitors: Liquipedia Dota 2 random distribution page; lxsmnsyc/PRD
notes: Demand is shown by two modest questions, one of which (economy balancing) is only adjacent. Could be folded into DicePool Lab as a mode. No dedicated web calculator showed up in my search, but the mechanics are well documented, so differentiation is the exact-statistics UX.

name: Rare Sky Events Almanac
idea: Searchable almanac of planetary transits, mutual occultations and eclipses for any observer body over centuries, precomputed and filterable in the browser.
description: Browse or filter long-range lists of transits, occultations and eclipses (Earth and other planets as the viewpoint), with exact timing, visibility by location where relevant and links to compute custom windows in the browser. Aimed at amateur astronomers, science writers and worldbuilders. Hard to copy because it needs validated ephemeris computations cross-checked against published catalogues, but the output is a static dataset that is cheap to host.
capital_note: Domain only; computation done on the developer's own machine at build time.
why_hard_to_copy: Domain-expert computation (mutual events seen from other planets, accuracy over centuries) validated against catalogues; not something a generic vibe-coded page can get right.
web_delivery: Build step precomputes events into static JSON served from Vercel hobby; browser filtering and optional custom search with astronomy-engine in a web worker.
satellite_what: Embeddable widget showing the next transit, occultation or eclipse and a countdown.
marketing_where: Astronomy Stack Exchange answers; Cloudy Nights forum; Astronomy club newsletters; Worldbuilding Stack Exchange
marketing_target: Amateur astronomers, science educators and worldbuilders
marketing_funnel: Search for a rare event -> almanac entry page -> custom search -> embeds
cold_outreach: Offer astronomy clubs a yearly rare-events sheet for their newsletter.
post_ideas: Every Venus-Jupiter occultation to 2100 | Transits seen from Mars: a calendar | Where did savage-garden.org go? A modern replacement
competitors: Project Pluto assorted events; timeanddate Mercury transit list; Wikipedia list of mutual planetary eclipses
notes: Small audience and several free tables already exist (Project Pluto, timeanddate); the gap is filter/search UX and non-Earth viewpoints. Two low-engagement requests two weeks apart.

name: Mistria Farm Planner
idea: A tile-accurate drag-and-drop farm layout planner for Fields of Mistria, shareable by link.
description: Players of the farming sim Fields of Mistria want to plan their farm layout before placing and decorating in game, as Stardew players can. The planner would hold hand-measured footprints for buildings, crops, paths and decor, and the fixed anchors (farmhouse, shrine), with undo, layers and a share link. Hard to copy because the footprint and rule data must be measured and verified in game.
why_hard_to_copy: Needs a hand-verified dataset of tile footprints and placement rules for each object, plus patch tracking; generic grid editors do not have it.
web_delivery: Static React/canvas app on Vercel; layouts saved as compressed JSON in the URL, optional Supabase table for named saves.
satellite_what: Searchable table of every placeable object and its tile footprint.
marketing_where: Fields of Mistria Discord and community forums; Steam discussion threads; Bluesky and X game hashtags; Wiki talk pages
marketing_target: Fields of Mistria players who plan layouts and decorate.
marketing_funnel: Cheat sheet in search results, then the planner, then the share link posted in Discord.
cold_outreach: Message popular layout-sharing players asking to import their screenshots as template layouts.
post_ideas: Plan your Mistria farm before year 1 (free tile planner) | Every Mistria object by tile size | Template layouts from the community
competitors: fieldsofmistria.it.com farm layout guide; Fields of Mistria wiki (wiki.gg)
notes: One post. A grid editor is a weekend job; the defensible part is the verified footprint data and keeping up with patches. Game-specific audience size is unknown.

name: Crossover Issue Finder
idea: Pick two comic characters and see every issue they both appear in.
description: A reader wants a site like a DC character guide that lists all appearances of a character and also lists the comics two characters share. This is a join over a character-appearance dataset, with fuzzy name merging and reading-order links.
why_hard_to_copy: Cleaning and merging character-appearance data from open sources (aliases, versions, teams) is the work; the query itself is trivial.
web_delivery: Next.js + Supabase Postgres with a pre-built appearance table; queries run server side.
marketing_where: Comic collector forums and Discords; Bluesky/X comics community; Podcast communities
marketing_target: Comic readers building reading lists.
marketing_funnel: Pair pages in search, then lists.
cold_outreach: Offer reading-order lists to comic bloggers.
post_ideas: Every issue where these two heroes team up | Rare crossovers of two characters
competitors: Grand Comics Database
notes: One post. Data licence and availability must be checked (Grand Comics Database licence terms were not verified).

name: Hours Any Day
idea: A web reader for the Liturgy of the Hours that opens any past or future date with the correct calendar rules.
description: A user who missed two days through illness could not open them in the app she uses, which only goes back one day. A web app would compute the liturgical day correctly (season, feast precedence, psalter week, local calendar) and show the prayers for any date, installable as a PWA with offline caching. Correct calendar logic is the hard part.
why_hard_to_copy: Liturgical calendar precedence rules (Easter computation, solemnities vs memorials, national and diocesan proper calendars) are correctness-critical and rarely implemented well; offline PWA.
web_delivery: PWA on Vercel hobby; calendar rules computed client-side; texts stored as static JSON or in Supabase.
satellite_what: Enter any date and see the season, feast rank and color for the chosen calendar.
marketing_where: Catholic Twitter/X and Bluesky; Parish staff and music director forums (for example musicasacra.com); Catholic app directories
marketing_target: Laypeople and clergy who pray the Hours and want free access to any date.
marketing_funnel: Calendar lookup search traffic, then the reader.
cold_outreach: Offer the calendar lookup to parish-tech newsletters.
post_ideas: Missed a few days? Open any date of the Hours | Why the calendar differs by country, explained with the rules
competitors: Universalis; DivineOffice.org (per forum thread)
notes: One post. New niche 'Faith & Religion' because no canonical niche fits. Big risk: the official English breviary texts are copyrighted, so a launch needs public-domain or openly licensed texts or a licence; check this first.

name: Gran Screen
idea: A caregiver-managed big-button home page for older relatives: only the links, audiobooks, radio, video-call and photos you choose, installable from the browser.
description: Adult children report that parents struggle with logins, two-factor flows and modern sites, and that off-the-shelf senior tablets or kiosk apps are native and costly. Gran Screen is a PWA home page with large tiles for the few sites and media the family chooses, remotely edited by a caregiver, with ad-free simple games and a daily 'I am fine' tap. It cannot lock down a device like a native kiosk app; the plan is to be the lightest option that works on any tablet already in the house.
why_hard_to_copy: Weak: simple to rebuild. Differentiation comes from caregiver-side remote control plus carefully usability-tested defaults for 80+ users, which takes real testing with seniors rather than code.
web_delivery: Installable PWA on Vercel; Supabase stores each household's tile list and caregiver permissions; media is links/streams only, no hosting of audio or video.
marketing_where: Caregiver and family tech-support communities; Senior centre and library tech-help volunteers; Hacker News Ask threads about seniors; Local council on aging newsletters
marketing_target: Adult children who act as tech support for a parent or grandparent.
marketing_funnel: Setup page for the relative's device -> caregiver adds tiles remotely -> weekly family photo/message tile.
cold_outreach: Offer library tech-help volunteers a free setup template for the patrons they assist.
post_ideas: The five tiles my 84-year-old father actually needs | Why sign-in is the real barrier for older users | Set up a tablet in ten minutes without app stores
competitors: Tech Ease; GrandPad; Homer Audio Player
notes: Strong repeated pain (three independent threads) but native senior launchers already exist and a web page cannot kiosk-lock a device. Treat as an accessibility-flavoured family tool, not a hardware replacement.

name: SignFinder
idea: Identify an unfamiliar foreign road sign by describing its shape, colour and symbols.
description: User picks shape, background colour, border and symbols (or answers a short wizard) and gets matching signs with meaning, country or region variants, and a link to the source. The moat is the tagged sign dataset including unusual local signs (height-limit pictograms, regional warnings) rather than only the standard Vienna Convention set.
why_hard_to_copy: Hand-tagged dataset of signs with searchable visual attributes; image-based sign recognition is not available for free and generic searches return random pages.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel; sign metadata and tags in Supabase; images hotlinked from Wikimedia Commons with attribution (no image hosting).
marketing_where: Travel Stack Exchange (answer sign questions); Driving-abroad forums; Expat Facebook groups; Wikimedia Commons community (as attribution partner); Show HN
marketing_target: Tourists driving abroad, expats, hire-car customers
marketing_funnel: Search 'what does this <country> road sign mean' -> sign detail page.
cold_outreach: Contact hire-car blogs and expat driving-licence guides.
post_ideas: What the pictograms on Spanish motorway signs mean | 10 road signs that surprise tourists in Central Asia | Search road signs by shape and colour
competitors: SignPath: Learn Traffic Signs (China-focused study app)
notes: Three high-view questions (2,424-3,868 views) but only one Q&A site. The Australian sign is a local sign, not a pictogram. Dataset creation is large; image licences (Commons attribution) must be handled; unclear willingness to return after one lookup, so it is mostly an SEO play.

name: AncientKeys
idea: A browser input method for ancient and historical scripts (polytonic Greek, Old Norse, Coptic, cuneiform) with transliteration typing, sign pickers and copy/share.
description: Someone asks for a keyboard app that supports extinct languages such as Ancient Greek, Old Norse, Sumerian and Coptic. AncientKeys is a PWA input method: type Beta Code or plain transliteration and get correct polytonic Unicode, pick Old Norse/Old English letters, search cuneiform signs by reading or sign name, and save snippets. The moat is the linguistic input rules and sign-list data, which general keyboards lack.
capital_note: Domain name only; Supabase free + Vercel hobby cover hosting
why_hard_to_copy: Correct Unicode normalisation for polytonic Greek, Beta Code conversion and sign-list mapping (Sumerian readings to cuneiform) needs scholarly data and testing.
web_delivery: Static PWA on Vercel with client-side transliteration engine and bundled sign lists; optional saved snippets via Supabase.
satellite_what: Paste Beta Code or transliteration and get polytonic Greek Unicode back.
marketing_where: Textkit forums; Lemmy c/languagelearning and c/history; Classics and Assyriology Discords; Old Norse and Old English study groups
marketing_target: Students and hobbyists of classical, Norse, Coptic and cuneiform languages
marketing_funnel: Converter page -> multi-script pad -> saved snippets
cold_outreach: Offer it to bloggers who write guides on typing ancient Greek
post_ideas: Type polytonic Greek on any phone without installing a keyboard | Search cuneiform signs by Sumerian reading | Old Norse letters cheat sheet with an input pad
competitors: OpenL Ancient Greek Keyboard; Keyman; Branah Coptic Keyboard
notes: Search found good Greek and Coptic web keyboards, but none for Old Norse or cuneiform. Single signal; the mobile-keyboard request could only be partly met by a web page (no system-wide keyboard).

name: DateCodeDecoder
idea: Decode lot and date codes printed on food packages by brand.
description: User enters a brand and the stamped code and gets the likely production or expiry date, using a crowd-curated table of per-manufacturer formats (Julian dates, plant codes, month letters) plus links to shelf-life guidance. The moat is the crowd-built format library, which does not exist in one place; manufacturers publish only fragments.
why_hard_to_copy: Community- and expert-curated library of brand-specific code formats; each entry needs real packages as evidence.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel; format rules (pattern, example, source) in Supabase; decoder runs in the browser.
marketing_where: Cooking Stack Exchange; Food safety and grocery-shopping Facebook groups; Consumer forums; Product Hunt
marketing_target: Shoppers checking reduced items and old pantry goods
marketing_funnel: Search '<brand> date code meaning' -> brand page.
cold_outreach: Ask consumer-advice writers to contribute formats.
post_ideas: How to read the date code on <brand> products | Julian date codes explained with 10 examples | Reduced-price shelf: is it actually expired?
competitors: Hormel: code dates decoded
notes: One signal with little engagement (266 views, 5 score). Dataset-driven moat, but demand evidence is the weakest in my set; included as an honest low-confidence idea.

name: Wall Planner Maker
idea: Print a yearly or monthly wall planner on A4/A3 with your country's public holidays, school terms and personal events.
description: Choose region, year, week start and layout (year-at-a-glance by week, monthly, term planner), import a personal ICS file or type events, then download a vector PDF. Region data covers public holidays, school terms and religious dates (Easter, Hijri, Hebrew, lunar). Moat is the curated regional holiday and school-term dataset and the layouts, not the PDF generation.
why_hard_to_copy: Curating accurate school-term and holiday data by region, handling movable and lunar dates and getting print layouts right is slow data work; the PDF layout alone is easy to copy, so the moat is honest-but-moderate.
web_delivery: Static web app on Vercel generating PDFs client-side (pdf-lib); region datasets as static JSON; saved layouts optionally in Supabase.
satellite_what: Free subscribable calendar feeds of school terms and public holidays per region.
marketing_where: Parent Facebook groups and school newsletters; Teacher communities (TES forums, teacher Facebook groups); Pinterest planner boards; Hacker News Show HN; Home-education forums
marketing_target: Parents, home-educators, teachers and anyone who plans on paper.
marketing_funnel: Free planner PDF -> premium layouts and saved regions.
cold_outreach: Offer a ready A3 term planner for a school's region to teacher and PTA communities.
post_ideas: Free A3 school-year wall planner with your state's term dates | Year-at-a-glance by week: why it beats a monthly calendar | Import your ICS file and print it
competitors: Neatnik one-page calendar; Tim van de Vall calendar generators; SLANZA annual wall planner; TeachStarter term wall planner; Print-ready calendar PDFs (ChatGPT app)
notes: Many printable-calendar sites exist, so only the combined holiday + school-term + ICS import in a generator is an opening. Holiday and school-term data must be refreshed yearly; sourcing licences for school-term data varies by country.

name: SwapSession
idea: Scheduled language-exchange sessions in the browser with fair half-and-half timers, goal-based matching and no dating-style profiles.
description: Tandem and Speaky reviewers say the apps feel like dating apps full of fake profiles, that multi-language use was easier before, and some were banned with no explanation. SwapSession matches people by language pair, level and time zone, books a time, opens a peer-to-peer video room in the browser with a timer that splits the hour between the two languages, and keeps profiles light with no photo-first browsing. Moat is the matching and scheduling quality plus trust features, but a cold-start network problem is the real risk.
capital_note: Domain plus possible small TURN relay cost if free STUN is not enough for some networks.
why_hard_to_copy: Time-zone and level matching with session scheduling, reputation and reporting; network effects in a language-pair niche. The cold start is hard for the builder too.
web_delivery: Next.js app on Vercel; Supabase auth, scheduling tables and Realtime for signalling; WebRTC peer-to-peer video so no media is hosted.
marketing_where: language learning Discord servers; Lemmy language-learning communities and language-learner forums; university language-club mailing lists; YouTube polyglot comment communities
marketing_target: Serious adult learners who want structured speaking practice.
marketing_funnel: Post a language pair and availability -> get matched -> weekly slot.
cold_outreach: Message university language clubs and conversation-hour organisers to run sessions on the platform.
post_ideas: A language exchange that books a time instead of chatting for weeks | Fair-time timer: 30 minutes each language | Exchange without profile photos
competitors: Tandem; HelloTalk; Speaky
notes: Cold-start and moderation costs are the main doubts; video via WebRTC can fail behind strict NATs without a relay.

name: Routine Boards
idea: Free web builder for printable and on-screen visual schedules and first-then boards for children who are non-verbal or autistic.
description: Parents of children who rely on picture schedules describe laminated cards and velcro boards as hard to manage and impossible to take along. Routine Boards lets caregivers build a day schedule or first-then board from an open pictogram library or their own photos, print it at true card sizes and use the same board full-screen on any tablet. The moat is a licensed, well-organised symbol set and print layouts, plus offline use.
capital_note: Domain only; symbol libraries chosen must be free and licence-compatible.
why_hard_to_copy: Curation and correct licensing of an open pictogram set, plus print layouts matched to real laminate/velcro card sizes and offline reliability, are more careful than a generic to-do board. Weak against apps from the same builder.
web_delivery: Next.js PWA on Vercel; boards stored in Supabase with photos kept small or local; offline caching with a service worker; print CSS for card sizes.
satellite_what: Pick two pictures and print a first-then card at the right size in seconds, with no account.
marketing_where: Autism parent and teacher Facebook groups; Special-education teacher communities and Teachers Pay Teachers audiences; Occupational therapist forums; Product Hunt
marketing_target: Parents, special-education teachers and therapists of children who need visual supports.
marketing_funnel: Free printable card -> saved boards -> shared with school or respite carers via link.
cold_outreach: Offer therapists a free board set for their top five routines.
post_ideas: Visual schedules without the laminator | Getting a picture routine to work for school and home alike | Check the licence before you use that pictogram
competitors: MyVisualRoutine; First & Then
notes: Signals come from the maker of a competing native app, so demand is plausible but not independently quantified. Check pictogram licences (several popular sets are non-commercial) and keep any photos of children out of server storage by default.

name: CognateMap
idea: Pick two languages and get cognate and false-friend lists with the regular sound-shift rules (like -tion to -cion), plus practice and text highlighting.
description: A learner argues that related languages share thousands of near-identical words and wants a tool that, given two languages, lists them and highlights them in a text. CognateMap would precompute cognate pairs from open etymology data, group them by sound-correspondence rules, mark false friends, and highlight likely cognates in pasted text. Moat is the curated rule sets and false-friend lists, which are expert work.
capital_note: Domain name only; Supabase free + Vercel hobby cover hosting
why_hard_to_copy: Needs hand-checked sound-correspondence rules and false-friend lists per language pair; naive string similarity gives wrong answers.
web_delivery: Precomputed JSON per language pair served statically from Vercel; matching and highlighting client-side; optional accounts in Supabase.
satellite_what: Paste a sentence and see words that look like your language but mean something else.
marketing_where: Lemmy c/languagelearning; Language learning forums; Linguistics Discords
marketing_target: Learners of a language related to one they know
marketing_funnel: False-friend checker -> pair explorer -> practice mode
cold_outreach: Share with polyglot bloggers who write about cognates
post_ideas: The sound-shift rules that unlock thousands of French-English words | False friends between Dutch and German that will embarrass you | Highlight the words you already know in any French text
competitors: Language Transfer
notes: Single signal and the original poster's framing is loose. Check existing cognate resources (Wiktionary etymology, language-specific lists) before building.

name: Disc Edition Database
idea: A community database of physical film releases (editions, barcodes, special features), like Discogs but for movies.
description: A collector wants a Discogs-style site to see every physical release of a film. The site would hold one page per edition with barcode, region, cuts, extras and packaging, and let users add copies to a collection or wantlist. Barcode scanning runs in the browser camera.
why_hard_to_copy: The edition database itself: community-curated, cross-linked by barcode, with a moderation process; code is not the moat.
web_delivery: Next.js + Supabase; barcode lookup in browser with a JS decoder; no image hosting beyond small cover thumbnails.
satellite_what: Enter a film and compare known releases side by side (cut, region, extras).
marketing_where: Physical media collector forums and Discords; Bluesky/X physical media communities; Letterboxd lists
marketing_target: Blu-ray, 4K and boutique-label collectors.
marketing_funnel: Edition comparison pages in search, then free accounts to track a collection.
cold_outreach: Ask forum collectors to seed one label's releases.
post_ideas: Every edition of one cult film compared | Which boutique labels have the most complete cuts
competitors: Movie Collector Shelf
notes: One post. I did not verify other existing physical-media databases (such as Blu-ray.com); the scorer should check how well they cover this before rating.

name: Play It Online Board Games
idea: A directory of which board games can be played online with friends, on which platform, free or paid, and how good the implementation is.
description: A user asks whether anyone has built a repository of all board games playable online with friends. The directory would map each game to its online implementations, price, player counts, supports voice and async play, and user ratings of the implementation quality. It links out to the platforms, no game engine hosted.
why_hard_to_copy: The cross-platform dataset (which game is on which of the dozen platforms and how it plays) is hand-curated and goes stale, so ongoing curation is the moat.
web_delivery: Next.js + Supabase; filterable table with user-submitted implementation records; no real-time play hosted.
satellite_what: Enter group size and platform access, get games you can play online right now.
marketing_where: Board game Discords; BoardGameGeek forums; Bluesky/X tabletop tags
marketing_target: Friend groups playing remotely.
marketing_funnel: Game night picker then directory.
cold_outreach: Ask board game podcasts to share the picker.
post_ideas: All the 4-player games you can play for free in a browser | Where to play game X online
competitors: FreeBoardGames.org alternatives list; Best sites to play online board games with friends
notes: One post, posted the day of my search. The idea is plausible but is mostly editorial curation.

name: Doctor Supply Atlas
idea: A state-by-state view of licensed physician counts and where they trained.
description: One user asks for a website tracking the number of licensed physicians by state and which medical schools they graduated from. The app would merge public state medical board statistics into one comparable dataset with charts and downloads. State formats differ, so the data work is the product.
why_hard_to_copy: Requires normalising fragmented public board data across states into a consistent schema, updated periodically; a one-off scraper does not stay current.
web_delivery: Precomputed aggregates in Supabase (well under the 500 MB free limit) with static charts on Vercel.
marketing_where: Health policy and data journalism communities; Medical education forums; Open data newsletters
marketing_target: Journalists, researchers and policy staff.
marketing_funnel: Chart pages in search, data download.
cold_outreach: Pitch one state comparison to data reporters.
post_ideas: Which states depend most on physicians trained abroad | Physician counts by state, one chart
competitors: Med School Mapper (Robert Graham Center); Texas Medical Board statistics
notes: One post. Heavy one-off ETL work and coverage may be partial; this is a niche research tool, not a mass-market app.

name: SafeSettings
idea: A family checklist and tracker of every parental-control setting across kids' services (Discord, Roblox, Minecraft/Microsoft, YouTube...), curated, dated and linked.
description: A parent with several kids' apps finds each service has its own controls, terminology and login and wants one place to manage or at least see them. A web app cannot control other services, but it can hold a hand-curated, date-stamped settings database per platform, generate a per-child checklist by age, deep-link to each settings page and flag when a platform changes its controls. The moat is the maintained settings dataset and change tracking.
capital_note: Domain name only; Supabase free + Vercel hobby cover hosting
why_hard_to_copy: A hand-maintained, verified-on-date settings database that tracks platform changes; generic AI answers go stale and are often wrong.
web_delivery: Next.js app with curated markdown/JSON data per platform on Vercel; per-family checklists and reminders in Supabase (no kid data beyond first names/ages).
satellite_name: Is My Kid's Discord Locked Down?
satellite_what: Five-minute interactive checklist for one platform with screenshots and dates.
marketing_where: Parenting forums and Facebook groups; Lemmy c/parenting; School PTA newsletters; Local library digital literacy workshops
marketing_target: Parents of 8-15 year olds with gaming and chat accounts
marketing_funnel: Single-platform checklist -> family profile -> change alerts
cold_outreach: Offer the data to parenting bloggers as an embeddable checklist
post_ideas: Roblox, Discord and Minecraft: the 12 settings to check tonight | Why parental controls are three logins per kid | What changed in Discord Family Center this month
competitors: Google Family Link; Canopy Discord guide; Salfeld Minecraft guide
notes: Two weak signals. The tool is information, not enforcement, so it may feel thin to parents wanting actual control. Maintenance burden of the data is the real cost.

name: FreeBusy Hub
idea: Combine all your calendars into one subscribable feed that shows only busy blocks, with a per-calendar choice of what details to reveal.
description: Paste the private ICS links of your work, personal and family calendars; the service expands recurring events correctly and publishes a single secret feed URL (and a small availability page) that shows 'busy' or selected details only. Aimed at people who juggle work and private calendars, freelancers, and families that share one availability view. The moat is correct recurrence and timezone handling across messy real-world feeds.
capital_note: Domain only; fetch-on-demand feeds fit free quotas at small scale.
why_hard_to_copy: Correctness-critical iCalendar handling: recurrence expansion, timezone definitions, all-day and multi-day edge cases, and CLASS/transparency fields that vary between providers.
web_delivery: Vercel serverless route fetches the user's source ICS URLs on request with short caching, expands events (RRULE, EXDATE, timezones) and returns a filtered ICS; Supabase stores account and feed settings; configuration UI is a normal web app.
satellite_what: Paste an ICS link or file and download a busy-only version, processed in the browser.
marketing_where: Hacker News Show HN; Product Hunt; AlternativeTo; productivity and freelancer communities; Mastodon calendar and privacy hashtags
marketing_target: Remote workers with work and private calendars, small teams, families
marketing_funnel: Scrubber tool -> sign up to keep a live feed -> share availability link
cold_outreach: Reply to calendar-sharing threads on forums with the live-feed alternative.
post_ideas: Share your availability without sharing your dentist appointment | One link that merges Google, Outlook and iCloud as busy-only | Why copying events between calendars keeps breaking
competitors: SYNCDATE; Sync Them Calendars; OneCal; SavvyCal merge guide
notes: Users must hand over secret ICS URLs, so trust and security design matter. Several sync tools address the same pain with different mechanisms. Strongest evidence is the single Nextcloud thread, not independent projects.

name: Night Shift Baby Log
idea: A shared baby tracker PWA that works offline at 3am, handles daylight-saving time properly, plots WHO growth percentiles, and lets parents add their own event types.
description: Two or more caregivers log feeds (including which breast was last), sleep, diapers, medication doses and custom events such as reflux or bath, all synced in real time and usable offline. Shows wake windows, growth percentile charts and a one-page summary for the paediatrician. Aimed at new parents who do not want ads or a paid sharing tier. The moat is correct time handling plus real-time offline sync and growth-chart data.
why_hard_to_copy: Offline-first sync with conflict handling for running timers, DST/timezone-correct durations, and percentile (growth chart) data and calculations.
web_delivery: Offline-first PWA on Vercel; Supabase Realtime and Postgres for multi-caregiver sync; local queue in IndexedDB for offline logging; growth percentile tables bundled as static data.
satellite_what: Free page: enter baby age, get typical wake windows and nap counts.
marketing_where: parenting forums and Facebook parent groups; Product Hunt; AlternativeTo; Pinterest newborn checklists; Hacker News Show HN
marketing_target: New parents and co-parents sharing night shifts
marketing_funnel: Wake window calculator -> create baby profile -> invite partner
cold_outreach: Offer doulas and midwives a free hand-out with a QR link.
post_ideas: Log a 3am feed one-handed, even offline | Why your baby app gets daylight saving wrong | Free paediatrician summary page from your logs
competitors: BabyApp (Baby Tracker & Sleep); BabyTrack; Baby Feeding Tracker; Baby Buddy
notes: Many app-store competitors exist; the open web-based gap and self-hosted demand is the angle. Individual requests are small. Health-adjacent data needs a privacy policy.

name: Pull Log
idea: A pull and collection logger for card and gacha games with per-account hit-rate stats.
description: Fans of rhythm and card games want a place to log which cards and costumes they own, as an older tracker did for another franchise, and card pack openers want to track packs opened per account with hit percentages to see who is lucky. One logger per game with a curated card list and optional shared community pull-rate statistics would serve both.
why_hard_to_copy: Per-game curated card/costume data and crowd-sourced pull statistics only matter at volume; each game needs maintenance.
web_delivery: Next.js + Supabase; per-game card datasets as static JSON; users log pulls manually or via CSV paste.
marketing_where: Game Discords; Fan communities on Bluesky/X; Fandom wikis
marketing_target: Players of gacha and trading card games.
marketing_funnel: Card list pages, then a free log.
cold_outreach: Ask fan-wiki editors to link the tracker.
post_ideas: Track every card you own for game X | Community pull rates after 10,000 logged packs
competitors: Pocket Tactics Project Sekai card list
notes: Two posts about different games. Unverified: sekai.best and other fan sites may already cover the first request (my search could not confirm what they offer).

name: Base Exit
idea: Check how hard it is to leave Airtable and import an Airtable export into Supabase tables with real relations.
description: Upload (locally) the CSV export of an Airtable base. The tool detects linked records, select fields and attachments, scores the migration complexity, and generates a Supabase/Postgres schema plus import script. Aimed at small teams, clubs and shops hit by the Bending Spoons takeover and layoffs. Moat is the field-type mapping rules, not the UI.
why_hard_to_copy: Mapping Airtable field semantics (linked records, rollups, lookups, multi-select, formulas) to relational tables with correct foreign keys is domain-specific; low moat otherwise, other migration tools exist.
web_delivery: Static web app on Vercel parsing CSVs client-side; outputs SQL and a Supabase import script; optional one-click import with the user's own Supabase project keys kept in the browser.
satellite_what: Free page that scores a local CSV export for migration difficulty (links, attachments, formula fields).
marketing_where: Hacker News Airtable threads; Supabase Discord and GitHub Discussions; Indie Hackers; AlternativeTo (Airtable alternatives)
marketing_target: Small teams and nonprofits with Airtable bases who want a cheap Postgres home.
marketing_funnel: Free score -> free schema generator -> hosted migration help.
cold_outreach: Comment on 'leaving Airtable' threads with the score tool.
post_ideas: How complex is your Airtable base to migrate? Score it in your browser | Airtable linked records to Postgres foreign keys, explained | Leaving Airtable for Supabase free tier
competitors: Grist; Baserow
notes: Demand evidence is thin (one real thread plus two supply-side posts) and Grist/Baserow already ship importers. Treat as a feature/satellite for a bigger Supabase product rather than a standalone business.

name: Trip Log
idea: A travel log that imports saved places from Google Maps exports and GPX files, with per-visit notes, time-zone-correct itineraries and a calendar feed.
description: Drop a Google Takeout saved-places file or GPX tracks and see them as visits on a map, attach notes to each visit rather than the place, and build multi-day itineraries where every leg shows the correct local time. Export the plan as a calendar file. Aimed at travellers who keep lists in Google Maps and want a structured record. The moat is the import parsers and time-zone-correct itinerary logic.
why_hard_to_copy: Obscure export format parsing done entirely in the browser plus timezone-aware multi-leg itinerary logic.
web_delivery: Web app on Vercel; Takeout and GPX parsed client-side; maps via free open tile sources; Supabase stores trips as text/JSON with no heavy media hosting.
satellite_what: Drop your Takeout saved-places file and see all places on one map, filter by list.
marketing_where: travel blogs and forums; Mastodon travel hashtags; hiking and trail communities; Product Hunt; AlternativeTo
marketing_target: Self-planning travellers and hikers who keep lists in Google Maps
marketing_funnel: List viewer -> save as trip -> itinerary and calendar feed
cold_outreach: Pitch travel bloggers a free way to publish their saved places.
post_ideas: See all your Google Maps saved places on one page | Plan a multi-timezone trip without losing track of local times | Per-visit notes: remember what you ate each time
competitors: AdventureLog; Wanderer; TREK; Wanderlog
notes: Crowded category. Demand evidence comes from one self-hosted project. I did not verify exactly what Google's current export format contains.

name: Club Shelf
idea: A book-club hub that works for the whole club even when members use different reading trackers: ranked polls, club TBR with votes, RSVPs and a club-wide ratings leaderboard.
description: Book-club organisers on StoryGraph keep asking for ranked or multi-pick polls, a shared club TBR members can upvote, several admins, club stats and a leaderboard that includes members who are not on the platform. Club Shelf is a standalone web app where the organiser creates a club, members join by link with no account, and each member can optionally upload their StoryGraph or Goodreads CSV export to prefill ratings and 'who has this on their TBR'. Voting maths (ranked choice, approval) and CSV-export parsing are the technical core.
capital_note: Domain only; Supabase and Vercel free tiers, Open Library API is free.
why_hard_to_copy: Moderate at best: ranked-choice/approval voting correctness, tolerant parsing of StoryGraph and Goodreads CSV exports (edition-agnostic matching of books) and club-level stats are real work, but a basic polls-and-RSVP club app is weekend-copyable (Bookclubs already exists).
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel Hobby, Supabase free for clubs/polls/RSVPs (row-level security per club), Open Library API for book covers, CSV parsing client-side; installable PWA.
satellite_what: Free no-login ranked-choice poll for picking the next read; paste titles, share link, see Condorcet/IRV result.
marketing_where: StoryGraph community forums and Discord servers; Goodreads group admins; Facebook book-club groups; Product Hunt; Library book-club coordinators
marketing_target: Volunteer organisers of 8-40 member book clubs, especially ones migrating off Goodreads
marketing_funnel: Free ranked poll link shared with the club -> members see the club page -> organiser creates a club
cold_outreach: Message club admins who posted public feature wishes: 'built this for the exact polls and co-admin gaps you listed'.
post_ideas: How our 30-person club picks books with ranked-choice instead of a messy group chat | Free ranked-choice poll for book clubs, no signup | We turned our members' Goodreads exports into a club leaderboard
competitors: Bookclubs (bookclubs.com); StoryGraph Book Clubs; Book Club by BookMovement
notes: Strong, current, multi-user signal (comments dated through Aug 2026) but a competitor (Bookclubs) already covers polls and RSVPs, so the pitch must be cross-tracker import plus club stats. StoryGraph has no public API, so import relies on the user-uploaded CSV export. Vote counts on the listing are unlabeled; stated as counters, not confirmed votes.

name: PlainRSVP
idea: Invite and RSVP page for bigger parties that works for every guest without an Apple ID, with spreadsheet import and name-based non-responder tracking.
description: Apple Invites reviewers complain that guests are tracked by email address, that Android and non-iCloud guests cannot open or answer invitations, and that you cannot import a spreadsheet or a Contacts group when you invite dozens of people. PlainRSVP gives each host one public link plus per-guest links, bulk import from CSV or vCard, household and plus-one handling, meal or dietary questions, and a 'who has not answered' list shown by name with copy-paste nudge texts. Moat is thin: the value is in guest-list import/dedup logic and polish, not in anything a determined vibe coder could not build.
capital_note: Domain; email reminders fit free tiers at this scale.
why_hard_to_copy: Honestly weak: Partiful already offers no-app RSVP. Only guest-list import and household/dedup logic, plus wedding-style extras (meal choice, seating), give a small edge.
web_delivery: Vercel-hosted web app with Supabase tables for events, guests and responses; guests only open a link, no install or account; email reminders via Supabase/Resend free tier.
satellite_what: Paste or upload a messy guest list and get deduplicated households, plus-ones and a clean CSV.
marketing_where: wedding and baby-shower planning forums and Facebook groups; Pinterest party-planning boards; Product Hunt; school and church event organiser groups
marketing_target: Hosts of 30+ guest events (weddings, milestone birthdays, reunions) and mixed iPhone/Android crowds.
marketing_funnel: Guest list cleaner -> create invite -> share link.
cold_outreach: Reply to people publicly complaining that Apple Invites guests could not open their invite with a link to a no-account alternative.
post_ideas: Import your whole guest spreadsheet and see non-responders by name | RSVP page that works for Android and grandma | Why your invite app should not require an iCloud email
competitors: Partiful; Apple Invites; Evite
notes: Strong, recent, multi-review signal, but low moat and a well-funded rival (Partiful). Worth it mainly as a wedding or large-guest-list niche play.

name: Bench AI-Free
idea: A browser Python classroom where the teacher watches students' code live, AI is absent, and no student accounts or installs are needed.
description: Teachers create a class with a join code; students code in a Pyodide-based editor that runs entirely in the browser (no server execution), and the teacher sees all editors in a live grid, can broadcast starter code, freeze submissions and restore snapshots. No AI assistant exists to turn off. Moat is the real-time sync and classroom workflow rather than the editor.
why_hard_to_copy: Real-time multi-editor sync with teacher control, offline-safe snapshots and sandboxed in-browser execution is non-trivial; but PyTogether and others already cover part of this.
web_delivery: Vercel-hosted app; Python runs via Pyodide in the browser; classroom state and live code sync through Supabase Realtime on the free plan; students join with class codes, no emails.
satellite_what: Free in-browser Python editor with shareable run links and no AI.
marketing_where: Hacker News Show HN; Computer science teacher communities (CSTA); Teacher Discords and Mastodon; Python education mailing lists; Product Hunt
marketing_target: High-school and college intro programming teachers who cannot control AI in existing tools.
marketing_funnel: Free single-class use -> paid for multiple sections and snapshot history.
cold_outreach: Email CS teachers who posted about disabling AI in Replit/others.
post_ideas: A Python classroom with no AI button to turn off | Watch every student's code live without walking the room | Pyodide in school Chromebooks: what works
competitors: PyTogether; CSUK:Coder+; Replit forum thread: disable AI for class; Code.org AI settings
notes: Three comments in one thread and a Replit forum complaint; PyTogether is a free open-source competitor, so differentiation must come from classroom management. School network filters may block Supabase realtime websockets.

name: Upkeep Planner
idea: A home maintenance planner where recurring chores are generated per appliance and per season, and the next due date counts from when you actually did it.
description: Add the appliances and parts of your home, pick from a hand-curated library of maintenance tasks with sensible intervals, and get a calendar with reminders that reschedule from completion. Also tracks lent-out items with return reminders. For homeowners and renters who find general to-do apps too dumb for recurring care. The curated task library and correct recurrence rules are the moat.
capital_note: Domain; email sending stays inside free quota at small scale.
why_hard_to_copy: A hand-curated, region- and climate-aware task and interval library plus a recurrence engine that handles 'after completion', seasonal windows and skipped cycles.
web_delivery: PWA on Vercel with Supabase auth and Postgres; reminders via email using Supabase scheduled functions or push for installed PWAs; task library shipped as JSON seeds.
satellite_what: Free page: enter home type and climate zone, get a printable spring/fall checklist.
marketing_where: Product Hunt; AlternativeTo; first-time homeowner Facebook groups and forums; Pinterest checklists; DIY and home-improvement YouTube comment sections
marketing_target: New homeowners and landlords
marketing_funnel: Printable checklist -> sign up to get reminders
cold_outreach: Offer free setup for small property managers.
post_ideas: The 12 things your furnace and water heater want each year | Smoke detector batteries and 9 other chores you forget | Why 'every 3 months' should start from when you did it
competitors: Hearth (iOS); Life Maintenance; HomeKeep (iOS); Homebox
notes: Engagement on the top thread is real but the other signals are thin. Several iOS competitors exist, so the angle is a web/PWA product with a better curated library.

name: Shared Private Journal
idea: A shared journal for couples, families or travel groups where entries are encrypted in the browser so even the host cannot read them.
description: Create a journal, invite a partner or family, and write entries that are encrypted with a key shared only among members, with a recovery option. Entries can carry a place so a map view shows where memories happened. Aimed at people who want a private shared diary without paying for Day One's premium. The moat is trustworthy multi-member end-to-end encryption and key recovery done right in the browser.
why_hard_to_copy: Multi-user key management, invitations, rotation and recovery are security-critical and easy to get wrong; most vibe-coded clones skip real encryption.
web_delivery: Web app/PWA on Vercel; WebCrypto for client-side encryption with per-journal keys wrapped per member; Supabase stores only ciphertext; photos kept small and limited to stay in free storage.
satellite_what: Single private note page encrypted with a passphrase, no account.
marketing_where: privacy-focused communities and newsletters; Hacker News Show HN; Product Hunt; AlternativeTo; couples and long-distance relationship forums
marketing_target: Couples, families and travel groups who want a private shared diary
marketing_funnel: Encrypted notebook page -> create shared journal -> invite partner
cold_outreach: Pitch to privacy-tool roundups and journaling bloggers.
post_ideas: A shared diary the host cannot read | Journal together on a trip without a premium subscription | How the keys work in a browser-encrypted shared journal
competitors: Day One Shared Journals; Memkeep; Sharing Me; Couples Relief
notes: Security claims must be audited before launch; reputational risk if keys are mishandled. Demand evidence is from two small self-hosted journaling projects plus competitors' premium gating.

name: Scene Soundtrack Lookup
idea: A crowd-sourced database that tells you where a song was used in a film, show or fashion runway show.
description: Two users want to look up whether a song appears in a film and to find the music for runway shows. A community-edited site with timestamps per scene and sources would answer both. Start with runway shows, which have no obvious dedicated database.
why_hard_to_copy: A curated, moderated, timestamped dataset with contributors is the moat; cold start is brutal.
web_delivery: Next.js + Supabase with edit history and moderation queue; track and film metadata linked out, no audio hosted.
marketing_where: Fashion communities on Bluesky/X and Tumblr; Music discovery forums; Film soundtrack fans
marketing_target: Fashion and film fans who chase song IDs.
marketing_funnel: Song pages in search, then contributors add scenes.
cold_outreach: Seed with one fashion week season and ask fan accounts to extend it.
post_ideas: Full soundtrack of one fashion week | Songs from one director's films by scene
competitors: Tunefind; WhatSong / What Is That Song?
notes: Two posts about slightly different media. Tunefind and others already serve film and TV; only the runway angle looks open. Moat depends on community.

name: FracPlan
idea: A free browser floor-plan drawer that accepts exact fractional-inch and mixed-unit dimensions, then shows a simple 3D view for furniture layout.
description: A home decorator found existing floor-plan tools too imprecise: one cannot take a wall length like 9/16 of an inch, another disables the field, and the paid cloud ones cost money. FracPlan is a 2D wall editor with exact fraction/metric entry, snapping and constraints, plus a basic 3D extrusion and furniture blocks. The moat is the unit-parsing and constraint-based geometry, which is real CAD-style logic.
capital_note: Domain name only; Supabase free + Vercel hobby cover hosting
why_hard_to_copy: Exact rational-number geometry, wall joins and constraint editing are non-trivial and easy to get subtly wrong.
web_delivery: Canvas/WebGL editor in the browser; plans saved as JSON in Supabase; no server compute.
satellite_what: Add, subtract and convert feet, inches, fractions and metric with a tape-measure style display.
marketing_where: Lemmy c/diy and c/homeimprovement; Woodworking and renovation forums; Interior-decorating hobby groups
marketing_target: Homeowners and DIYers planning rooms or furniture layouts
marketing_funnel: Fraction calculator -> room sketch -> saved plans
cold_outreach: Offer to renovation bloggers
post_ideas: Plan a room with true 9/16 inch measurements | Free floor-plan tool that doesn't round your walls | Layout a bedroom before buying furniture
competitors: Sweet Home 3D; Floorplanner
notes: Weak engagement (3 points); crowded category. Only worth building around the exact-fraction entry angle.

name: Fingerspelling Reader
idea: Installable offline PWA for practising reading fingerspelling (BSL two-handed, Auslan, ASL) at adjustable speed.
description: Learners see words fingerspelled by a clean hand animation at chosen speeds, type what they read, and progress through word lists by level, all cached offline so it works on airgapped phones and planes. Teachers can share word lists by link. Hard to copy only through assets: original, community-reviewed handshape animations for several sign languages are the work, the code is simple.
capital_note: Domain only; assets produced by the developer.
why_hard_to_copy: Original handshape assets for multiple sign languages with Deaf-community review; honestly the software is easy, the assets are the moat.
web_delivery: PWA on Vercel hobby with a service worker caching SVG/animation assets; progress stored locally; Supabase free optional for shared word lists.
marketing_where: Sign language learner groups on Facebook and Discord; Local BSL and Auslan class teachers; Linguistics Stack Exchange
marketing_target: Sign language learners, interpreters in training and teachers
marketing_funnel: Free practice page -> install as app -> share a custom word list with a class
cold_outreach: Offer sign language tutors a free, installable practice tool for their students.
post_ideas: Practise fingerspelling reading offline (installable) | BSL vs ASL fingerspelling speed drills | Make a custom fingerspelling word list for your class
competitors: Auslan fingerspelling practice game; Sign Language Forum BSL fingerspelling game
notes: Very thin (49 views, one asker). Free online games already exist, so the delta is offline install plus multiple sign languages. Likely a small, non-commercial niche; flag low market size.

name: Plant Care Library
idea: A free plant care library with watering, light and soil guidance per species, plus reminders that adapt to your room and season, usable as a plain web app.
description: Search a species (or pick from a curated starter list), add the plant to a room, and get care reminders with intervals based on light, pot size and season rather than a flat every-7-days. Includes pet-toxicity flags and a 'what went wrong' checker for yellow or drooping leaves. Aimed at houseplant owners who find paid apps pushy. The moat is the curated species care dataset, not the app shell.
capital_note: Domain only; dataset compiled from open sources by hand.
why_hard_to_copy: Hand-curated and verified care dataset with adaptive interval rules; external plant APIs used by self-hosted apps have proved unreliable or paid.
web_delivery: PWA on Vercel; species dataset as static JSON built from open data (e.g. open plant databases) and hand-checked; Supabase for user plants and reminders; email or web-push reminders.
satellite_name: Is This Plant Safe For My Pet?
satellite_what: Free lookup of common houseplants and whether they are toxic to cats and dogs.
marketing_where: houseplant forums and groups; Pinterest; Product Hunt; AlternativeTo; plant-swap and gardening club newsletters
marketing_target: Houseplant owners who dislike subscription plant apps
marketing_funnel: Pet-safety lookup -> save plant -> care reminders
cold_outreach: Offer local plant shops a QR care-card per plant sold.
post_ideas: Your plant does not need water every Sunday | Which common houseplants are safe for cats | A plant care list that works without an app store
competitors: HortusFox; Water me; Gardenia; Plant Parent / Planta
notes: Dataset effort is the real cost for a solo developer and licensing of source data needs checking. Evidence is from two small self-hosted projects.

name: Fan Gallery Hub
idea: A link-based gallery of fan art and fan merch for one creator's community, with credits to the original artists.
description: A VTuber with commissioned and gifted art wants a gallery showing the pieces with credit to each artist, and a fan wants an online artist alley compiling all fan-made merch for a talent group. A hub that stores links, credits and tags (not image files) lets communities browse by artist, character and merch type.
why_hard_to_copy: Community curation and permissions (artist opt-in, takedown handling) in one fandom; weak technical moat.
web_delivery: Next.js + Supabase table of entries (external URL, artist handle, tags); previews through official embeds or thumbnails; no image storage.
marketing_where: VTuber Discords; Bluesky/X fandom tags; Fan wikis
marketing_target: VTubers and fan communities.
marketing_funnel: Creator makes a free hub, fans submit links.
cold_outreach: Offer to set up a hub for small VTubers.
post_ideas: Credit every fan artist in one page | Online artist alley for talent X
competitors: Notion credit pages kept by streamers; DeviantArt
notes: Two thin posts and easily copied; moat is only the community. Include only if the scorer wants a community-led idea.

name: Porch Board
idea: Email-first community board for neighbourhood associations and small clubs: members get a digest and can post by email or web, admins moderate in one queue.
description: Groups leaving Facebook say older members will not learn Slack or forums, CC-list emails are a mess, and forum software with email notifications 'dies fast'. Porch Board keeps email as the main interface (weekly digest, reply-to-post where possible) with a simple web page for admins to approve posts, pin notices and publish a public info page. The honest moat is thin: it depends on admin-led adoption inside small groups rather than technology.
capital_note: Domain only; inbound email processing would need a free tier of an email provider.
why_hard_to_copy: Weak: any developer can build a forum. Defensibility would come only from email-first threading/digest design that works for 70+ members and group-by-group adoption, i.e. small-niche network effects.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel; Supabase Auth with magic links and RLS per group; digest emails via a free-tier email API on a scheduled function; public group page is a static route.
marketing_where: Neighbourhood association and HOA admin groups; Local club secretaries; Hacker News Ask/Show threads about leaving Facebook; Library and community-centre bulletin boards
marketing_target: Volunteer admins of neighbourhood, hobby and parish groups.
marketing_funnel: Admin creates a group from a pasted email list -> members receive the first digest -> posting by email.
cold_outreach: Offer to migrate one neighbourhood's CC list into a moderated list in an evening.
post_ideas: We left Facebook for our street group: what worked for the over-70s | Why forum software dies in small communities | Fixing the CC-list newsletter
competitors: Facebook Groups / Nextdoor; Spond; Jonline; Discourse
notes: Real, repeated pain but the weakest moat in the file; included for the 'older members will only use email' insight. Reply-by-email (inbound parsing) is not guaranteed on free tiers; fall back to one-click reply links.

name: DryRoute
idea: Road-trip planner that lines up forecast rain with your ETA at each point along the route and suggests a later departure or alternative route.
description: A driver asked for an app that combines driving directions with weather to show where it is not raining along a 600-mile route. DryRoute samples the route at the time you will actually be there, shows precipitation and wind along the timeline, and compares departure times or routes. Moat is the time-aligned sampling (ETA per segment against hourly forecasts) and free-tier public APIs, not a pretty map.
capital_note: Domain name only; Supabase free + Vercel hobby cover hosting
why_hard_to_copy: ETA-aligned forecast sampling across alternative routes and departure windows, with caching to stay inside free API quotas.
web_delivery: Map UI (MapLibre) in a Next.js app; routing and forecast calls proxied through Vercel serverless functions with caching; saved trips in Supabase.
satellite_what: Enter origin, destination and a date range and see the driest departure hours.
marketing_where: Lemmy c/travel and c/cycling; Road-trip and RV forums; Motorcycle and van-life communities; Festival and wedding travel groups
marketing_target: Long-distance drivers, motorcyclists and cyclists planning around rain
marketing_funnel: Departure-window finder -> route weather -> saved trips
cold_outreach: Pitch to motorcycle touring clubs that plan group rides
post_ideas: How we chose our departure time for a 600-mile drive by rain radar | The driest route is not the shortest: a worked example | Free tool for choosing your road-trip start time
competitors: Drive Weather App; Magic Earth
notes: Existing apps cover this; the edge would be departure-time optimisation. Check free-tier terms of weather and routing APIs for commercial use (Open-Meteo free tier is non-commercial; US NWS data is free).

name: Table Captions
idea: A shared live-captions page for small gatherings: one phone listens, everyone else reads the text on their own screen.
description: Hearing-aid users say restaurants, parties and group conversations remain hard even with aids, and people build captioning tools for hard-of-hearing family members. Table Captions turns any phone browser into the microphone and shows large, speaker-labelled text on any screen via a join code, aimed at church groups, clubs, family dinners and small meetings. It relies on the browser's built-in speech recognition for the free core.
capital_note: Domain only; Web Speech API is free in supporting browsers.
why_hard_to_copy: Weak. A vibe coder can wire the Web Speech API in a weekend; the only defensible parts are reliable multi-device sync, readable caption styling for hearing loss and group-friendly speaker labelling.
web_delivery: Next.js PWA on Vercel; Web Speech API in the speaker's browser; Supabase Realtime broadcasts text to joined viewers; no audio is stored or uploaded to our servers.
marketing_where: Hearing-loss support communities (HLAA-style local groups); Church accessibility committees; Club secretaries who host meetings; Hacker News Show HN
marketing_target: Hard-of-hearing people and the groups that include them.
marketing_funnel: Host opens a room link -> guests join by code -> optional saved transcript.
cold_outreach: Offer a local hearing-loss support group a free trial at their next meeting.
post_ideas: Live captions for the whole table with just a browser | Setting up captions at a club meeting without new hardware | What captions can and cannot do in noisy rooms
competitors: Rylo Live Transcribe; Ava; Windows Live Captions
notes: Browser speech recognition quality and support vary (Chrome and Safari work best) and may send audio to the browser vendor's servers, which must be disclosed. Native tools are strong, so this only fits the group-sharing niche. Optional paid speech APIs could improve accuracy later.

name: GadgetRecipes
idea: Find recipes by the kitchen equipment you own rather than by ingredient.
description: A community-tagged index of recipe links by equipment (meat grinder, ice cream maker, pasta extruder, bread machine), filterable and linked out to the original source so no recipe text is copied. The moat is the community-curated tag set; search engines return product pages and low-quality content for 'recipes using X'.
why_hard_to_copy: Community-curated equipment tagging of links (a small-network effect), not machine-generated; but a thin moat until it has contributors.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel; Supabase tables for recipe links, equipment tags, votes; no image hosting.
marketing_where: Cooking Stack Exchange; Appliance owner Facebook groups; Kitchen gadget forums; Product Hunt; Show HN
marketing_target: Owners of specialty kitchen equipment
marketing_funnel: Search 'recipes for <gadget>' -> equipment page.
cold_outreach: Invite appliance-owner group moderators to seed tags.
post_ideas: What can you make with a meat grinder besides sausage? | Bread machine: 20 recipes beyond loaves | Share your best recipe for an ice cream maker
competitors: Instant Pot Eats air fryer recipes
notes: Single signal (371 views, 4 score). Included only because the stated gap (no equipment filter) was confirmed by search; a vibe coder could build the shell quickly and the moat is community, so treat as speculative.
